leadParagraphs: In 2024, Public Skills Australia identified nine megatrends impacting the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors. These megatrends were further considered in the development of the 2025 Workforce Insights Reports .

While these megatrends will continue to have longer term implications for workforce planning and development across the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors, the 2026 Workforce Insights Reports have built on these and analysed four key drivers of change that cut across most megatrends. This is important as these drivers of change will likely impact the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors in the short to medium term. The four key drivers of change include:

These megatrends were identified in previous Workforce Insights Reports and will continue to have longer term implications for workforce planning and development across the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors.

blocks.title: The four key drivers of change
blocks.intro: Select any driver below to read the analysis and cited sources.

items.title: Driver 1 — Resilience of organisations to respond to strategic shocks
summaryParagraphs: Organisational resilience is emerging as a critical driver of change across Australia's Public Safety and Government industry-sectors, particularly as agencies confront increasingly frequent and complex strategic shocks. Recent experience with compounding crises (such as increasingly intense bushfires, major cyber attacks and intensifying geopolitical tensions) have exposed structural vulnerabilities and highlighted the need for more adaptive, anticipatory and integrated capabilities. Investment will be required to deepen organisational capabilities that supports system-wide preparedness, robust governance and the ability to maintain critical functions under stress.2

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Sources (2): Australian Government Department of Home Affairs, Organisational Resilience: Good Practice Guide, Australian Government Department of Home Affairs, 2024, accessed 25 February 2026.

items.title: Driver 2 — Challenges to workforce productivity
summaryParagraphs: In its Five Pillars of Productivity inquiry reports, the Productivity Commission observed that productivity growth has been slowing globally since the mid-2000s, with Australia experiencing the slowest productivity growth in 60 years. The Productivity Commission identified long-standing pressures that have contributed to the productivity slowdown, including market stagnation, a persistently tight labour market and slower uptake of technological innovations.3 These factors are further exacerbated by emerging challenges linked to the megatrends including an ageing population, technological development, climate change and competition for labour.4

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Sources (3, 4): Productivity Commission, Five pillars of productivity inquiries – final reports, Productivity Commission, 2025, accessed 13 February 2026 · Productivity Commission, Five pillars of productivity inquiries, Productivity Commission, 2025, accessed 25 February 2026.

items.title: Driver 3 — Emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), greater automation and broader digital transformation
summaryParagraphs: AI, automation and accelerated digital transformation are powerful drivers of organisational and system-level change in the short term. This is reinforced by a push from the Federal Government for greater adoption of AI and digital initiatives across federal agencies.5 These initiatives signal a shift toward embedding AI into core service delivery, regulatory functions and operational decision making. AI, automation and digital transformation represent an opportunity for significant capability uplift through AI-enabled analytics, automation of high-volume processes and advanced digital platforms that enhance situational awareness, threat detection and emergency response coordination. Conversely, they represent a growing security risk as they are also being leveraged by threat actors to disrupt government services, facilitate foreign interference, enable disinformation, promote false narratives through deepfakes and erode trust in government institutions.6

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Sources (5, 6): Australian Government Department of Finance, National framework for the assurance of artificial intelligence in government, 2024, accessed 25 February 2026 · Australian Government Digital Transformation Agency, Policy for the responsible use of AI in government, 2025, accessed 25 February 2026 · Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO), Director-General's Annual Threat Assessment 2025, ASIO, 2025, accessed 25 February 2026.

items.title: Driver 4 — Workforce inclusivity
summaryParagraphs: Workforce inclusivity has been a key focus across the labour market. In the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors this is likely to translate into a continued focus on recruiting, retaining and developing employees from diverse cultural, linguistic, gender, disability and neurodivergent backgrounds. As organisations seek to increase workforce participation from these cohorts, they will be required to adapt and change legacy systems and processes to respond to the needs of the modern workforce.

cards.title: Limitations in career pathways
cards.summary: Career pathway opportunities for young professionals require further promotion, as potential employees are often unaware of Local Government career opportunities and pathways.

cards.title: Climate change
cards.summary: Climate change impacts many functions of Local Government, such as emergency management and environmental planning.

cards.title: Competition for labour
cards.summary: Local Government is competing for labour with the private sector and other parts of the public sector. There is also competition for labour between Local Government organisations.

cards.title: Expansion of core duties
cards.summary: Local Government employees are increasingly taking on multiple roles to meet community needs in the Local Government industry sector.

cards.title: Diversity and inclusion
cards.summary: Equitable gender composition and meaningful participation of a diverse workforce is an ongoing goal for Local Government workforces, particularly in leadership roles.

cards.title: Demographic shifts
cards.summary: Ageing workforces can impact the transfer of institutional knowledge and further create skills gaps in Local Government workforces.

cards.title: Technological development
cards.summary: The implementation of new technology in the Local Government workforce can be impacted by resource constraints and the availability of training.

cards.title: Recruitment and retention
cards.summary: There are several barriers to the attraction and retention of Local Government workforces in remote, regional and rural locations.

cards.title: Public trust and perceptions
cards.summary: Local Governments are required to balance resourcing constraints with meeting community needs, which can impact public trust and perception.

content.headerTitle: Federal and State/Territory Government Industry-Sector Overview
leadParagraphs: In Australia, all tiers of government play an essential role in governance and delivery of public services. The Federal Government is responsible for both domestic, economic and foreign affairs, while state and territory governments provide state or territory-based services, in line with relevant legislation, including but not limited to health, education and criminal justice.

paragraphs: Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report

As there are a breadth of roles across the public sector, several occupations are in the remit of other JSCs, such as early childhood educators and allied health professionals. Other occupations that make up the public sector including Defence, Police and Local Government will be covered in other Workforce Insights Reports produced by Public Skills Australia.

The 2026 Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report focuses on non-frontline occupations that support the business of Federal and State/Territory Government such as, but not limited to, policy analysts, project management, inspectors and regulatory officers and project administrators. As each Federal and State/Territory Government is unique, the following sections provide a snapshot of each workforce as well as any relevant industry insights to provide context for the overarching workforce challenges.

In the subsequent sections that follow, data profiles have been created to present the workforces for the Federal and State/Territory Government industry-sector. These data profiles primarily refer to the public service where such data is available, noting that, in some jurisdictions, data is only available for the broader public sector. Public Skills Australia notes that these figures are likely to include front-line roles including but not limited to, police, health and education-based roles.

blocks.title: Federal Government Overview
paragraphs: The Federal Government is made up of 102 agencies and 198,529 Australian Public Service (APS) employees (Federal Government workforce, as of 30 June 2025).[[7]] While a large proportion (35.4 per cent) of APS employees are based in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT), APS employees are spread across Australia, with a considerable proportion based in Victoria (18 per cent), New South Wales (16.9 per cent) and Queensland (13.3 per cent). The APS workforce is diverse with women comprising a large proportion of employees (60.5 per cent).[[8]] First Nations employees comprise 3.4 per cent of the APS, however the Federal Government has committed to increasing First Nations employment to 5 per cent of the APS by 2030.[[9]] The following datapoints were identified through this industry overview for the Federal Government workforce:
agencies
Australian Public Service (APS) employees (Federal Government workforce, as of 30 June 2025)
women
First Nations employees - committed to increasing First Nations employment to 5 per cent of the APS by 2030
APS growth to 2030 and JSA employment projections to 2035

While the number of APS employees grew by over 13,000 (7.1 per cent) between 2024 and 2025, JSA projects this rate of growth to slow substantially, with 18,000 employees projected to join the workforce in 2030, at a growth rate of approximately 1.7 per cent per year.[[10]] Reporting by the Australian Public Service Commission (APSC) reported that 79% of agencies identified cyber security as a critical skills shortage, with identified critical skill shortages in 2025, and 64% identified critical skills shortages in enterprise/technology architecture.[[11]]
Skills shortages identified by APS agencies and the response

The Federal Government is strengthening workforce planning capability to meet future workforce needs. This includes the Delivering for Tomorrow: APS Workforce Strategy 2025, which has a range of resources to support workforce planning in the APS. The APS Academy also provides learning and development to build capability in the APS, allowing a pathway to address future skill gaps. They provide training in AI and other critical digital skills areas. Government priorities to build in-house capability compared to relying on external work provides an opportunity to address skills shortages internally among existing APS employees.
85% of respondents identified Digital and ICT skills as being in shortage
79% of respondents felt Cyber Security skills were the most lacking capability

The Australian Capital Territory Public Service (ACTPS) comprises approximately 31,825 employees.[[12]] ACTPS makes up approximately 11.6 per cent of the whole ACT workforce,[[13]] emphasising its position as a major employer in the territory. The workforce is predominantly female, with women accounting for close to two-thirds of employees. A small proportion of employees identify as non-binary.[[14]]

The ACTPS workforce is diverse with employees from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) backgrounds accounting for over 25 per cent of the workforce, 2.8 per cent of the workforce identifying as LGBTQIA+ and 3 per cent of employee's report living with a disability.[[15]]

In the ACTPS, First Nations employees account for approximately 2 per cent of the workforce, below the ACT Government's 3 per cent employment target by 2026.[[16]] Since 2020, the level of ACT public service employees who identify as First Nations has been consistent at around 2 per cent.[[17]]
The Australian Capital Territory Public Sector comprises the ACT Public Service (ACTPS), statutory bodies and agencies.

The ACTPS is governed by the Public Sector Management Act 1994 (PSM Act) and the Public Sector Management Standards 2016 and consists of nine directorates including Health, Education and Justice and Community Safety.
Separate to the ACTPS, there are 21 independent bodies that operate under section 152 of the Public Sector Management Act 1994.
Gender Pay Gap

Between 2023–24 and 2024–25, the ACTPS grew by 3.5 per cent,[[18]] which is greater than the projected 10-year employment growth project for the Public Administration and Safety Industry[[19]] in the ACT (16 per cent over 10 years).[[20]] The ACT Government has implemented several initiatives to build capability in the ACTPS and has committed to embedding a culture of continuous learning and innovation in leadership development to build a future ready workforce. This includes targeting entry-level recruitment through the ACTPS Graduate Program, which in 2025 transitioned to a career path model that supports balancing business needs and graduate capability.[[21]]

The ACT Skills Needs List identifies more than 150 occupational skills shortages. This list enables targeted workforce strategies by aligning in-need occupations and the VET qualifications that support them. The list includes two occupations split across five qualifications under the PSP Public Sector Training Package, which Public Skills Australia can address.[[22]]

paragraphs: Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report

subSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The New South Wales Public Service (NSWPS) employed approximately 84,780 full-time equivalent (FTE) employees in 2025.[[23]] The majority were engaged on an ongoing basis, with smaller numbers of staff employed on temporary or casual arrangements.[[24]] The workforce is geographically distributed, with more than 27,782 employees in regional areas,[[25]] emphasising the NSWPS as a major employer in regional areas.

The NSW Women's Strategy 2023–2026 identifies improving gender equality outcomes, including reducing the gender pay gap.[[26]] In 2025, women comprised 66.6 per cent of the NSWPS workforce, while men accounted for 33.3 per cent of employees.[[27]] A small proportion of employees identified as non-binary. Despite women representing a majority, the gender pay gap in the NSWPS stood at 7.3 per cent in 2025, an increase from 7.2 per cent in 2024.[[28]] Addressing this pay gap remains an ongoing priority for the NSWPS.
Diversity information indicates that employees who speak a language other than English comprise over one fifth of the NSWPS workforce.[[29]] Employees with disability comprise 2.8 per cent.[[30]]

First Nations people comprise four per cent of the NSWPS workforce,[[31]] above the New South Wales (NSW) Government's three per cent employment target by 2025 in non-executive salary levels, as set out in the NSW Public Sector Aboriginal Employment Strategy.[[32]]

subSections.title: Structure and Legal Context
paragraphs: The New South Wales Public Service (NSWPS) encompasses Departments, Executive Agencies related to a department, and Separate Public Service Agencies. The NSWPS consists of those employed under Part 4 of the Government Sector Employment Act (2013) (GSE Act). There are 11 departments of the Public Service, each led by a Secretary.

The Government Sector comprises the Public Services, Teaching Service, the NSW Police Force, the NSW Health Service, the Transport Service of New South Wales and any other service of the Crown. It also includes bodies constituted by an Act or prescribed by regulations, such as a State owned corporation. The NSWPS incorporates the government sector and other government agencies (e.g. the Independent Commission Against Corruption). These areas of government are defined by the GSE Act (2013).

paragraphs: Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report

subSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Queensland Public Service (QPS) comprises approximately 74,410.52 FTE.[[43]] The workforce is geographically dispersed, with close to two thirds employed in regional areas and one-fifth located in Brisbane's inner city.[[44]] Women represent most of the workforce, while men comprise just over one-third.[[45]] A small proportion of employees identify as non-binary or preferred not to disclose their gender.[[46]] Diversity data shows employees from CALD backgrounds as the largest cohort, followed by LGBTQIA+ and those with disabilities.

First Nations people make up a smaller (2.7 per cent) share of the workforce. Between 2021 and 2025, QPS saw gradual growth in First Nations peoples representation from 2.5 per cent to 2.7 per cent.[[47]] During this period the Queensland (QLD) Government increased its First Nations workforce target from 3 per cent to 4 per cent in 2023.[[48]] While the data indicates progress, a gap remains relative to the stated target, highlighting the continued focus required on First Nations employment. The QLD Government has established explicit employment diversity targets for CALD individuals and people with disabilities, with the target for both cohorts set at 12 per cent of the workforce.[[49]]

subSections.title: Structure and Legal Context
paragraphs: The QPS comprises Departments, Statutory Agencies related to a department, and separate Public Service Agencies. The Public Service consists of those employed under the Public Sector Act 2022. There are 22 departments of the Public Service, each led by a Secretary. The Queensland Public Sector comprises over 100 different organisations and involves delivering different services including education, healthcare, social welfare and public security.

subSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Tasmania State Service (TSS) comprises approximately 36,168 employees.[[58]] The workforce is predominately female, with women accounting for just over 70 per cent of employees, men comprise just under 30 per cent and 0.3 per cent identifying as 'other'.[[59]] Overall, the gender profile reflects a strongly female-dominated public sector workforce, similar to other states and territories.

Diversity data from the 2024 Tasmanian State Service Employee Survey shows variation across cohorts. Employees who speak a language other than English represent the largest diversity group at 11 per cent of the total workforce.[[60]] Eight per cent of employees were born overseas in another country and 6 per cent identify as LGBTQIA+.[[61]]

First Nations employees make up approximately 3 per cent of this workforce. While the Tasmanian Government had a set target to increase First Nations employment from to 3.5 per cent across the TSS, this only covered up to 2022 and does not appear have been renewed.[[62]]

subSections.title: Structure and Legal Context
paragraphs: The TSS comprises of 17 Agencies (for example, the Department of Premier, and authorities such as the Environment Protection Authority). The TSS supports the government of the day by providing robust and independent policy advice and ensures a wide range of services are delivered to the community. The TSS also provides support to Ministers to develop and implement policies and legislation, administer state finances, manage resources and deliver or support on a wide range of public services.

content.badge: Theme 1 · Future of the Public Service · Insight 1
leadParagraphs: As Australia's productivity growth remains relatively low, the effectiveness of the APS remains critical to supporting economic performance.

insightPager.label: Insight 1 of 3 · Future of the Public Service

paragraphs: Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report

Productivity growth in Australia has slowed in recent decades. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) observed that labour productivity growth in the five years preceding the COVID-19 pandemic was around half the average rate recorded over the previous 50 years.[[88]] The OECD highlighted lower productivity in the mining sector and the expansion of the Public Administration and Safety sector as key factors in this slowdown.[[89]]

However, whilst some analyses consider public sector growth to provide downward pressure on productivity growth, others identify how efficient public service workforces can contribute directly and indirectly to economic growth. In 2024-25, the Gross State Product (GSP) of states and territories grew by 1.4 per cent, which has been attributed to, in part, to the Public Administration and Safety industry.[[90]] In the ACT, increased public sector activity has been highlighted as a driver for GSP growth.[[91]] Alongside their direct impact on economic measures such as GSP, productive public sector agencies have a broader indirect influence on the economy through ties to the private sector. Public sector funding for education, the flow on benefits of public infrastructure projects, and efficient service delivery are examples of how public sector workforces can contribute indirectly to economic growth and productivity.

While it is challenging to capture the full impact of the public sector on productivity, reports from the ABS indicate that public demand, driven by government expenditure and investment, supports Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth.[[92]] Therefore, an effective and skilled public sector plays a critical role in supporting economic growth and productivity as it continues to expand.

There is a need to regularly upskill the public sector workforce for at least the next 5-10 years in technology, digital literacy and AI use, however this may shift as younger generations enter the workforce with those skills already. The public sector must remain agile to emerging skilling needs following the emergence of AI.

blocks.title: Workforce Gaps — occupations in shortage by jurisdiction

paragraphs: AI was identified as an emerging skills gap across the public sector consistently noting the need to uplift workforce capability to support future-ready service delivery.

Several stakeholders indicated that demand for digital, ICT and cyber-security skills, are the most critical shortages and are further compounded by increasing competition from the private sector for digitally proficient and highly skilled employees. Stakeholders highlighted that talent attraction and retention, particularly in digital and technical roles, is an ongoing challenge across the public sector.

Jurisdictional workforce strategies to respond to these requirements include: expanded VET funding, entry-level recruitment reforms and targeted capability programs such as the APS Academy, the ACTPS Career Path Graduate Model, NT digital skills boot camps and other diversity and capability initiatives.

leadParagraphs: A skilled, adaptable and future-ready public service workforce has been identified as a priority, particularly in relation to technology, digital literacy and effective use of AI.

insightPager.label: Insight 3 of 3 · Future of the Public Service

paragraphs: Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report

The 2025 Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report highlighted that each state and territory has different legislative requirements for workforce planning, and therefore different levels of workforce planning maturity. This theme remains prevalent in 2026, within the context of planning for the future of the public service, with changing expectations of government services, and trust in the public service.

Public Skills Australia intends to facilitate 'Future Skills for the Public Service' workshops to provide a forum for cross-jurisdictional knowledge sharing. Drawing on a strategic foresight approach, these discussions would identify shared skills needs and assess future skilling requirements across the public service. Public Skills Australia intends to examine how the VET system could be used or adapted to support these emerging workforce needs. Consultations with stakeholders indicated interest in, and support for, this approach, particularly given that each jurisdiction has different levels of workforce planning and understanding of skills and workforce needs.

paragraphs: The 2025 Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report proposed to further scope the development of a strategy to investigate the consistency of implementation and outcomes from traineeship and apprenticeship programs in each public sector. The objective of the proposal was to determine if the consistency, accessibility and effectiveness of VET traineeship and apprenticeship pathways into public sector roles across Federal and State/Territory Governments should be investigated, mapped and good practice of the implementation of the programs identified.

pages.title: Auslan, Interpreting and Translating Qualification Review

content.headerTitle: Auslan, Interpreting and Translating Qualification Review
leadParagraphs: In response to the 2023 Disability Royal Commission Final Report, Public Skills Australia has commenced a multiphase project to address the recommendation to improve access to Auslan language services. The aim of this project is to increase the number of Auslan interpreters and translators available to Federal and State/Territory Governments. This work supported the following strategic priorities:

paragraphs: Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report

blocks.title: Ministerial Priority 2026
paragraphs: The project will contribute to continuing to progress actions to consider and address barriers to participation in Auslan, interpreting and translating qualifications to support an increase in the number of qualified Auslan interpreters as identified in the final report from the Royal Commission into Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation of People with Disability.

blocks.title: Public Skills Australia Strategic Plan
paragraphs: Support industry-sectors through high-quality training products.

blocks.title: Drivers of Change
paragraphs: Challenges to workforce inclusivity.

Following in-depth consultation with Deaf community members and training provider representatives, the resulting Auslan Interpreting and Translating Final Report identified a range of challenges in the design and implementation of the qualifications. The findings and recommendations from Phase One will be actioned in Phase Two to address these key challenges identified and update the qualifications in accordance with the Training Package Organising Framework. Phase Two will see the redesign of the Training Package.

These reports are requirements under individual Federal and State/Territory Public Sector Acts.

Overall, these reports provide yearly data and insights about the public sector workforces in federal, state and territory public sectors, as well as any relevant workforce capability strategies or other relevant programs of work being undertaken to uplift the public sector.

items.title: APS Reform Program
summaryParagraphs: The Government's APS Reform Program (the Program) was established to strengthen the public service, under four pillars of public service transformation:
bullets: Pillar 1: The APS embodies integrity in everything it does
Pillar 2: The APS puts people and business at the centre of policy and services
Pillar 3: The APS is a model employer
Pillar 4: The APS has the capability to do its job well
In 2025 there was significant progress embedding key reform principles especially on investing in skills development and embracing digital technologies and AI to deliver services.

summaryParagraphs: The NSWPS Commission Strategic Workforce Planning Framework (the Framework) aims to assist agencies across the NSW Government sector to better understand and prepare for their future workforce needs.
The Framework outlines a practical, principles-based approach to implementing strategic workforce planning, which can be tailored to meet the circumstances and workforce needs of individual agencies.
The Framework has 5 stages of the planning cycle:
bullets: Align - align organisational strategy and Strategic Workforce Planning priorities
Compare - compare options to achieve outcomes
Implement - develop and implement the plan

The Plan focuses on essential skills in industries facing shortages, such as construction, digital, cyber and energy transition.
The Plan has five strategic priorities:
bullets: Priority 1: Target skilling responses to government priorities
Priority 2: Improve equitable outcomes, pathways and access for students
Priority 3: Strengthen industry and employer partnerships and skills governance
Priority 4: Build and support the NSW VET teaching workforce

summaryParagraphs: The NSW Aboriginal Employment Strategy 2019-2025 (the Strategy) was developed to build a culturally safe and capable NSW public sector that reflects the communities it serves, and where First Nations employees feel supported, respected, valued and empowered to pursue their career aspirations.

Initiatives in the 2024-25 Strategy focused on resources and initiatives to attract, retain and support a talented First Nations workforce and create inclusive and respectful workplaces for the First Nations workforce.
An independent review of the Strategy has commenced to assist in developing a successor Strategy for 2026 to 2030.

leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia's work is informed and guided by the Federal Government initiatives detailed in the table below.

items.eyebrow: National Cabinet (Formerly Council of Australian Governments)
items.title: National Agreement on Closing the Gap (Closing the Gap)
summaryParagraphs: Closing the Gap is a commitment from all Australian governments and First Nation peoples representatives, to a fundamentally new way of developing and implementing policies and programs that impact the lives of First Nations peoples. This includes policies and programs impacting recruitment, health and social programs specific to First Nations peoples, which are relevant to the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors.

Closing the Gap is jointly implemented by the Federal, State and Territory governments, along with Australian Local Government Associations and Coalitions of Peaks. It focuses on four priority reforms (strengthen formal partnerships and shared decision making; build the community-controlled sector; transform government organisations; and shared access to data) and 19 national socio-economic targets, covering areas such as life expectancy, education, employment, justice and child protection. Overall progress towards meeting Closing the Gap targets has been mixed. Implementation of Closing the Gap is ongoing to 2031. The Productivity Commission is tracking these targets.

Closing the Gap performs a substantive role in informing Public Skills Australia’s research and engagement efforts. Closing the Gap informed stakeholder consultation preparation as part of engagement for the 2026 Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report.

items.eyebrow: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
items.title: The Australian Government’s Strategic Priorities
summaryParagraphs: The Australian Government’s strategic priorities provide a four-year (2022-2026) policy direction for the APS and sets targets across key areas. These areas include the economy, public health and climate change.

The Australian Government’s strategic priorities are into the final year of their implementation by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet with relevant APS departments and organisations. So far the Strategic Priorities, which have not been placed on set timelines, have achieved several outcomes, including hosting a Jobs and Skills Summit, developing a plan for cheaper child care, implementing fee-free TAFE and creating more university places, establishing the National Reconstruction Fund, introducing legislation for a national anti-corruption commission and strengthening strategic partnerships in the Pacific and South East Asia. Progress is still required for public health and aged care, improving housing supply and planning reforms and advancing government budget sustainability.

The “strong inclusive and sustainable economy” priority informed Public Skills Australia’s approach to the 2026 Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report and provided important context for stakeholder consultation preparation. These priorities also supported the development of the Identify future skills needs for Federal and State/Territory Government project.

items.title: Working for Women – A Strategy for Gender Equality
summaryParagraphs: The Working for Women strategy outlines a framework for the Australian Government to improve national gender equality. It sets out five priority areas and reports on a range of outcomes and indicators annually to monitor Australia’s progress.
Specific to JSCs, Priority Area 3 focuses on improving gender pay gaps, supporting access to skills and training and reducing occupational and industrial gender segregation.

To date, the Australian Government has increased female recruitment into trades and other occupations through apprenticeship supports, fee-free TAFE and targets in the Australian Skills Guarantee, along with including gender equality as a national priority in the National Skills Agreement.

In March 2025, the Department for Workplace Relations launched the Advancing Gender Equality in Gender Segregated Industries grant program, directly linked to Priority Area 3. This grant program received a $28.5 million extension in December 2025.

Priority Area 3 of the Working for Women strategy – addressing economic equality and security – directly informed the requirement for, and development of, the proposed strategy Identify future skills needs for Federal and State/Territory Government. This work will seek opportunities to identify where any gender-based differences in future skills requirements may exist.

items.title: The Clean Energy Generation: Workforce needs for a Net Zero Economy
summaryParagraphs: This series of reports considers emerging and future clean-energy workforce requirements as Australia strives to reach net-zero emissions by 2050. JSA’s preliminary modelling estimates Australia’s clean-energy workforce will need to grow from the current 53,000 employees to 84,000 employees by 2050.

The report makes 50 recommendations to support governments in focusing their efforts on how skills shortages can be averted in the set time, resources and legislative constraints and government objectives. Broadly, the recommendations cover the issue areas of participation and attraction, hiring and retention, transitioning employees and communities, roles and responsibilities, critical occupations, education and training and transport. Implementation remains ongoing and long-term, aligned with the 2050 net-zero target.

This series of reports, specifically, the recommendations made within the reports, informed preparation for stakeholder consultation as part of research and engagement for the 2026 Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report. These recommendations provided context on where skilling and occupational priorities may exist in Federal, State and Territory Government workforces.

items.title: Australian Cyber Security Strategy
summaryParagraphs: The 2023-2030 Australian Cyber Security Strategy serves as a roadmap to achieve the Australian Government’s vision of becoming a world leader in cyber security by 2030.

The Strategy is structured around six ‘cyber shields’ (strong citizens and businesses, safe technology, world-class threat sharing, protected critical infrastructure, sovereign capability and resilient regional/global leadership). These are to be delivered in three stages or ‘Horizons’ (2023-2025 strengthening the foundations, 2026-2028 scaling efforts across the whole economy and 2029-2030 leading the development of new cyber technologies). Progress to date has been on the foundational aspects of the Strategy, with the initial work under ‘Horizon 1’ (2023-2025) concentrating on improving incident reporting and response mechanisms, introducing legislative reforms, piloting threat-sharing initiatives and raising government and critical infrastructure security standards. Overall coordination sits with the Department of Home Affairs, specifically through the Australian Cyber Security Coordinator. The remaining two horizons are to be implemented over the next four years up to 2030.

This ongoing cyber security work provided important contextual background for stakeholder consultation preparation for the 2026 Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report and informed the need for the Identify future skills needs for Federal and State/Territory Government. Specifically, cyber security roles are identified as a current critical skills need, and there is a requirement to determine whether this demand will persist into the medium to long-term future.

items.title: Unlocking the Potential of VET
summaryParagraphs: In March 2024, the Qualification Reform Design Group (QRDG) provided advice to Skills Ministers on reforming the VET qualifications system. This included advising that:

As a result, Public Skills Australia undertook a Demonstration Project that consulted widely to determine the efficacy of updating qualification and unit of competency templates. This report was delivered to the QRDG in Q3 2024.

In December 2024, the QRDG provided their final report and recommendations to Skills Minsters, based on national consultation and findings from the JSC Demonstration Projects. The recommendations from this report centred around modernising VET qualifications by implementing a purpose-led, principles-based approach to qualification design. As a result, JSCs are responsible for ensuring qualifications serve a clear purpose, are linked to workforce needs and are not unnecessarily duplicated.

The ongoing work of the QRDG regarding qualification reform continues to inform the method and intended outcomes for both the Review of Government Investigations Qualifications and Review of Procurement and Contracting Qualifications projects.

items.title: Occupation Standard Classification for Australia
summaryParagraphs: Formerly known as the Australia New Zealand Standard Classification of Occupation (ANZSCO), the Occupation Standard Classification for Australia (OSCA) is a standardised framework for classifying occupations in Australia. As part of the replacement process from ANZSCO to OSCA in 2024, the ABS announced that OSCA will undergo regular updates in accordance with the OSCA Maintenance Strategy, which was released in 2025.

Changes to OSCA outlined in the Maintenance Strategy involve stakeholder engagement and are timed to ensure that each Census of Population and Housing uses the most recent update. Under the Strategy, the first round of consultations and feedback with stakeholders on proposed changes to OSCA are scheduled to be completed in August 2026, with the next update to be published in March 2027 before the data release of the 2026 Census in October 2027.
Public Skills Australia continues to utilise, where possible, the most contemporary version of OSCA to ensure our occupational insights remain relevant and in-line with whole-of-economy standards.

items.title: Better Together – The Jobs and Skills Report 2024
summaryParagraphs: Better Together was released in November 2024 as part of JSA’s mandated obligations to provide insight on the Australian labour market and advice on workforce needs and priorities. It details evidence aligned to five strategic pillars to enable a more prosperous economic future, including:

Better Together outlines JSA’s key current and emerging datasets that provide useful insights on the intricacies of Australia’s labour market for use in development of strategic workforce planning for the JSCs. Please note JSA released an updated version of this iterative report in November 2025, Connecting for impact – The Jobs and Skills Report 2025, which will inform the 2027 Workforce Insights Reports.

The outcomes of Better Together provided important context on whole-of-economy skilling and training needs. Specific to the 2026 Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report, these outcomes informed the development of the Identify future skills needs for Federal and State/Territory Government proposed workforce strategy that aims to ensure this industry-sector maintains a future-ready workforce.

items.title: Occupational Shortage List
summaryParagraphs: The Occupational Shortage List (OSL), which was formerly the Skills Priority List, offers an annual point-in-time review of the status of Australian occupations. Specifically, the OSL reports on whether occupations (at the 4-digit and 6-digit ANZSCO level, and the 6-digit OSCA level) are experiencing shortages nationally and for each state and territory in regional or metropolitan areas.

The OSL was last updated in 2025. The latest OSL differed from previous iterations due to the fact that in 2024 the ANZSCO classification framework for occupations was replaced with the OSCA framework. In terms of the 2025 OSL results, it was reported that 29 per cent of occupations (293 out of 1022 assessed) were in national shortage, which was 4 per cent lower than 2024 (33 per cent) and more than 7 per cent lower than 2023 (36 per cent). The OSL in 2025 also added 29 occupations newly in shortage compared to 2024, most of which were roles related to health, science, technicians and trades and machinery operators and drivers. As of February 2026, JSA had started the 2026 OSL survey but it had not yet confirmed a publication date for this year's list.

The OSL provided important context for stakeholder consultation preparation for the 2026 Federal and State/Territory Government Workforce Insights Report. This list indicates on a national level where specific occupation demands currently exist and enabled Public Skills Australia to proactively pursue conversations with Federal, State and Territory Government stakeholders on whether these demands exist within their contexts.

leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia is the Jobs and Skills Council (JSC) for the Public Safety and Government industry, comprising Correctional Services, Defence, Federal, State/Territory and Local Government, Fire and Emergency Services and Police industry-sectors.

Through its work, Public Skills Australia actively supports employer and employee bodies in these industries and associated volunteer associations. Public Skills Australia works in partnership with the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR) and other JSCs to give effect to broader Ministerial and government priorities.

leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia's Workforce Insights Reports are developed using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data obtained from primary and secondary sources. This 2026 Correctional Services Report is supported by data obtained through stakeholder consultations and engagements.

paragraphs: Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report
These consultations were used to gain insight into challenges the Correctional Services industry-sector is facing in developing and maintaining a skilled workforce.

The challenges identified through these consultations were thematically analysed to identify shared challenges and trends. Specific to the Correctional Services industry-sector, and in alignment with the tripartite approach for JSCs, consultations were held with employers, employee bodies and Government organisations, both in-person and through online meetings, workshops and presentations.

Following these consultations, Public Skills Australia conducted secondary qualitative and quantitative research to verify the challenges raised. Additional targeted consultations with senior stakeholders were held to further validate workforce challenges and identify related industry insights.

blocks.title: Drafts were subsequently progressed through Public Skills Australia's governance process that includes:

subSections.title: 1 · Correctional Services Subcommittee
paragraphs: The Subcommittee is responsible for recommending this report to the Industry Advisory Group (IAG) for endorsement.
This recommendation is made on the basis that the Subcommittee is satisfied that sufficient consultation and engagement has been undertaken, and that consultation feedback was appropriately actioned.

subSections.title: 2 · Industry Advisory Group
paragraphs: The IAG is responsible for endorsing this report to the Public Skills Australia Board for approval to be submitted to DEWR.

This endorsement is made on the basis that the IAG is satisfied with the Correctional Services Subcommittee's recommendation for endorsement. The IAG further provides its strategic guidance and endorsement if comfortable that the strategic priorities of Public Safety industry-sectors are also captured.

subSections.title: 3 · Public Skills Australia Board
paragraphs: The Public Skills Australia Board (the Board) is responsible to approve the submission of the report to DEWR.

This approval is made on the basis that the Board is satisfied that an appropriate development and consultation process was followed and that the report has been progressed in line with the internal governance requirements of Public Skills Australia.

The Report uses publicly available datasets accessible from Jobs and Skills Australia (JSA), the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS), the National Centre for Vocational Education Research (NCVER) and other supporting online sources. Due to the complexity of large-scale workforce data, no single source provides an accurate or complete picture. Therefore, multiple data sources are used to provide the most accurate representation of the workforce as possible, supported by qualitative research (including interviews with stakeholders). This research was bolstered by literature reviews of government reports and documents, online sources, annual reports, departmental documentation, legislation, research articles and relevant Royal Commission Reports.

Qualitative research further included industry engagement undertaken for the Corrections Implementation Report and the Drivers for Recruitment, Attrition and Retention (Corrections) Report 2025. Consistent with the tripartite approach to industry engagement, Public Skills Australia engaged broadly through both consultation and surveys of Registered Training Organisations (RTOs), private and public employers, union representatives and a small number of current learners.

Public Skills Australia thanks the contributors, including industry representatives, its Board and governance group representatives, DEWR and Jobs and Skills Australia (JSA) for sharing their views and data generously, and supporting the development of this Report.

leadParagraphs: The Correctional Services industry-sector plays a critical role in managing offenders. The workforce spans a broad range of occupations, including COs, who deliver custodial services in corrections facilities, and CCOs, who supervise offenders serving non-custodial sentences or parole in the community. The workforce also includes public servants working inside and outside correctional environments across functions such as administration, education, health, policy and intelligence.

paragraphs: Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report

blocks.title: Workforce Growth vs. Demand
paragraphs: Trend 1

The Correctional Services industry-sector workforce has grown at an average rate of 4.3 per cent per annum over the past five years.[[10]] Despite overall industry-sector growth, the number of COs has decreased by 13.5 per cent over the same period, declining nationally from approximately 21,500 to 18,600.[[11]] The industry-sector workforce is projected to increase by 6.3 per cent over the next five years, and 11.2 per cent over the next ten years.[[12]] Therefore, the current rate of growth is not keeping pace with the increased number of individuals serving custodial sentences, which has risen by an average of 5.9 per cent.[[13]] Growth in custodial sentences may generate downstream demand for CCOs as persons in custody transition to parole.

blocks.title: Demand for Community Corrections
paragraphs: Trend 2

The number of individuals serving a community corrections order has increased, rising by 3.9 per cent since 2020, growing on average 1.5 per cent per year.[[14]] Recidivism rates tend to be lower for adults completing community orders (15.4 per cent returning to community corrections within two years) compared to persons in custody released from correctional facilities (44.5 per cent returning to correctional facilities within two years).[[15]] At the same time, the ratio of individuals serving community corrections orders per CCOs has decreased from 16.5 in 2015-16 to 15.4 in 2024-25.[[16]]

leadParagraphs: Recent trends across Australia's Correctional Services industry-sector underscore the growing importance of community-based supervision and the workforce required to deliver it. While previous Workforce Insights Reports focused primarily on the custodial setting, this report focuses on community corrections roles which form an increasingly critical component of the criminal justice system.

The numbers of persons serving community corrections orders has continued to rise in recent years with community corrections orders representing the largest category of correctional supervision nationally. Further, the offender-to-staff ratio remains substantially high across all jurisdictions, emphasising the workload carried by CCOs. Projected growth in the Correctional Services workforce, alongside substantial public investment in the industry-sector across states and territories further emphasises the need to better understand the workforce capabilities required to support community corrections.

paragraphs: Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report

subSections.title: Recruitment pipeline
paragraphs: Challenge 1

Correctional Services organisations face a range of perception-based challenges impacting workforce recruitment alongside key drivers resulting in high attrition rates including support structures for new prison officers, increased workload and career pathway limitations.

subSections.title: Implementation of VET training
paragraphs: Challenge 2
Challenges have been identified with the implementation of the Certificate III in Correctional Practice, the entry level qualification for the Correctional Services industry-sector.

blocks.title: Two 2025 projects
paragraphs: These projects focused on CO occupations in custodial settings rather than CCO occupations. Subsequently, the community corrections workforce became the primary focus for this Report. Stakeholder insights from the 2025 engagements, aided by further research, broadly identified that while CCO training is supported by the entry-level qualifications (Certificate III and IV in Correctional Practice), challenges remain with their implementation and delivery. This is being experienced and viewed in different ways by the industry-sector, with some reporting that the challenge was directly related to the qualifications and others reporting that it was related to how the qualifications are contextualised when implemented for training delivery. Both these perspectives will be considered to ensure that any mitigating strategies lead to the shared outcome sought by stakeholders.

The Drivers for Recruitment, Attrition and Retention (Corrections) Report 2025 examined public perceptions of working in the Correctional Services industry-sector and their impact on recruitment, attrition and retention. It identified five findings that will be considered by the Corrective Services Administrators’ Council (CSAC) in 2026. Further information about this Report can be found in the Workforce Insights: Update on 2025 Strategies section (and in the attachments to this Report).

insightPager.label: Insight 1 of 3 · CSC Correctional Services Training Package

paragraphs: Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report

blocks.title: The Role of a Community Corrections Officer (CCO)
paragraphs: The role of CCOs is to assess and manage risk, monitor compliance with legal conditions (such as bail, parole and sentencing requirements) and respond to breaches of such conditions. CCOs provide case management and risk assessment of people who are serving a sentence (custodial and non-custodial) and assist in the transition and reintegration of offenders from custodial settings back into the community. They support behavioural change and seek to reduce the likelihood of reoffending.

Through research and consultation, Public Skills Australia identified several distinct challenges that have implications for the workforce and training specific to CCOs across jurisdictions within the Correctional Services industry-sector.

blocks.title: A. Entry Level Training and Specialisations for Community Corrections Officers
paragraphs: Stakeholders noted challenges in accessing appropriate skills specialisations through the Certificate III in Correctional Practice for CCOs. These skills are captured in Adult and Youth Community Specialisations across both Certificate III and Certificate IV. However, consultations and data verified that organisations are electing to train CCOs through the Certificate IV in Correctional Practice rather than the Certificate III (due to specialisation units of competency in the Certificate III not providing the sufficient complex knowledge required for the role). In some jurisdictions, stakeholders reported that the skills possessed by CCOs are also becoming increasingly valued in the custodial environment for COs.[[19]]

blocks.title: Industry Insight
paragraphs: Community corrections roles require dynamic skills and are focused on rehabilitation and reintegration back into a community. This means that CCOs require the capability to support the reduction of recidivism and enable rehabilitation.

blocks.title: B. Career progression-related training
paragraphs: Career progression for CCOs and challenges in accompanying training was also highlighted as a significant challenge. As CCOs advance through the different government grades (or salary bands), with each level bringing greater complexity and responsibilities within their roles, stakeholders indicated that this progression often did not correspond with accredited skills development.

Consequently, most CCOs undertook further non-accredited training to augment their skill base in line with the increasing demands of their work duties. For management training especially, CCOs (and managers in the custodial systems) frequently returned to VET training to gain the necessary managerial qualifications at a higher Australian Qualification Framework (AQF) level in the Correctional Services Training Package.[[20]]

blocks.title: C. In-sector transition
paragraphs: Consultation with the Correctional Services industry-sector revealed that while transitions from community corrections to custodial roles were relatively uncommon, there were successful examples of COs transitioning to community corrections roles. Stakeholders reported anecdotal examples of employees shifting from CO roles to CCO positions, often after injury and as part of support for employee return-to-work plans.

COs who move into community corrections bring valuable experience in managing offenders within the custodial environment, and this background is viewed as a strong foundation for case management roles. However, this potential pipeline from CO to CCO roles is often constrained by the recruitment requirement for higher education qualifications, which may impact the eligibility for COs to apply.

blocks.title: Industry Insight
paragraphs: The CCO role is comparatively complex, often requiring an understanding of advanced concepts such as behavioural change, acceptance and commitment theory, trauma-informed response, alcohol and other drug treatments and training for dealing with sex offenders. As such, it is seen as more specialised than what the current Certificate III in Correctional Practice offers. Several jurisdictions reported that they only offered Certificate IV level training for CCO roles.

blocks.title: D. Regional recruitment
paragraphs: Alongside training challenges are a shortage of CCOs in regional and rural areas. Stakeholders have reported challenges in formulating job packages to attract recruitment outside metropolitan areas, especially given that regional locations vary in their appeal to potential recruits. Moreover, community correctional work in such areas often involves long-distance travel to remote districts, which makes it harder to attract potential recruits.

These distinctive characteristics of community corrections work underscores the need for workforce planning and qualification design that recognises the context-specific capability requirements across the corrections system from the custodial to community levels in regional settings.

Stakeholders noted that some organisations were electing to train CCOs through the Certificate IV in Correctional Practice rather than the Certificate III in Correctional Practice. Enrolments in units of competency for the Certificate III unique to community corrections specialisations are estimated at approximately 160, whereas enrolments in units of competency for the Certificate IV community corrections specialisations are substantially higher at approximately 300.[[21]] This is despite, as the graphs indicate, 4,234 more enrolments in the Certificate III compared to the Certificate IV in 2024.[[22]] Proportionally, significantly more people are enrolling in these specialisations in the Certificate IV compared to the Certificate III.

Low enrolments and completions in the community corrections specialisations are further compounded by some jurisdictions indicating that they also accept a relevant higher education degree in social sciences. In some jurisdictions, such qualifications are a condition of employment, while in others they are considered highly desirable but not required as a condition for employment.

blocks.title: CSC Correctional Services Training Package — challenges
paragraphs: Stakeholders generally supported all specialisations in both the Certificate III and IV in Correctional Practice; however, the following challenges were identified:
bullets: The Certificate III in Correctional Practice does not fully reflect the complexity of community corrections roles.

Certificates III and IV in Correctional Practice do not include emerging capability requirements such as trauma-informed practice, domestic and family violence, sex offenders in the community and mental health (including suicidal ideation).[[23]] As a result, some jurisdictions are utilising non-accredited training to bolster the VET qualifications.
Delivery of Certificates III and IV in Correctional Practice was identified by RTOs as challenging to contextualise for community corrections settings.

leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia’s 2024 Correctional Services Workforce Plan, identified two challenges impacting the Correctional Services workforce:
To support industry with these challenges, Public Skills Australia completed two projects in 2025 to provide deeper insights into their causes.

paragraphs: Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report

blocks.title: Demand Management
paragraphs: Project One

Correctional Services organisations face a range of recruitment, retention and attrition challenges, indicated by reduced employee numbers and increasing prison populations. This also manifests in attraction based challenges, relating to perceptions and stereotypical narratives about working in this industry-sector.

blocks.title: Workforce Mobility
paragraphs: Project Two

Correctional services organisations face challenges in relation to participation in the VET sector and particularly with the implementation of the Certificate III in Correctional Practice, the entry level qualification for Correctional Services.

leadParagraphs: The Drivers for Recruitment, Attrition and Retention (Corrections) Report 2025 (Drivers Report) examined public perceptions of working in the Correctional Services industry-sector and its impact on recruitment, attraction and attrition. This work supported several strategic priorities including:

paragraphs: Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report

blocks.title: Ministerial Priority 2026
paragraphs: Using strategic workforce planning and strong stakeholder engagement to continue building a shared, evidence-based view of the challenges and opportunities for industries and across JSCs.

blocks.title: Public Skills Australia Strategic Plan
paragraphs: Support industry-sectors to continue to build and maintain capable and mobile workforces that are future-ready.

blocks.title: Drivers of Change
paragraphs: Resilience of organisations to respond to strategic shocks.

blocks.title: The Drivers Report identified five findings and associated recommendations that were presented to the Corrective Services Administrators’ Council (CSAC) for consideration in 2026
rows: 1. Low awareness and outdated perceptions impact recruitment pools.

There is low awareness of and outdated perceptions about the Correctional Services industry-sector that impacts recruitment pools. Generally, respondents indicated that they often imagined Correctional Services through a custodial lens: uniforms, razor wire and surveillance rather than as a diverse professional field.
2. The potential recruitment pool for Correctional Services could be increased significantly if more information is accessible about the variety of careers.
Around one-third of respondents indicated they had ‘never thought about’ Correctional Services as a career option, signalling an awareness gap.
3. There are identifiable cohorts that could be targeted to improve Correctional Services recruitment pools.

Millennial female respondents presented an important diverse cohort when provided with targeted messaging addressing workplace safety concerns. Professional and degree-qualified respondents showed high receptivity to considering Correctional Services as a career. This was duplicated in respondent cohorts who held managerial roles.
4. Shifting narratives about Correctional Services changes perceptions and attitudes towards considering a career in this industry-sector.

Priority cohort respondents indicated that safety and meaningful impact messages resonated with them, particularly when supported by authentic workplace evidence. Respondents indicated that messaging effectiveness depends entirely on authenticity. Branding and communications without corresponding workplace improvements may simply increase the distance between promise and reality, ultimately undermining recruitment efforts.
5. Barriers to considering Correctional Services as a career were predominantly perceptual.

Respondents indicated that the strongest deterrents were fears about safety, emotional resilience and workplace culture, alongside uncertainty about personal capability. Respondents indicated that the perception of being judged by others was a deterrent, with nine per cent citing concerns about broader negative public perceptions and social stigma.

blocks.title: These findings were supported by the following recommendations:

paragraphs: Prioritise recruiting metropolitan Millennial males, Generation Z males and Millennial females.
Primary Outcome: Increased applicant pool.
Focus on opportunities to recruit professionals and managers into Correctional Services careers. Prioritise professionals and managers.
Primary Outcome: Quality candidates at all organisational levels.

Consider strategies to attract employees to relocate or commute to regional locations. Prioritise addressing the mismatch between the target cohort location (metropolitan focus) and facility location (predominantly regional), particularly in relation to commuting to and from work.
Primary Outcome: Improved regional facility recruitment.

Undertake targeted messaging campaigns that present the accurate and accessible information about working in Correctional Services. Prioritise rehabilitation focused narratives and genuine and authentic messaging as primary anchors, and sequence messaging to cohort types.
Primary Outcome: Reduced perception barriers and increased engagement.

blocks.title: Next Steps
paragraphs: Public Skills Australia is now engaging with CSAC to work through the implementation of the findings of the Report. The aim is to support the Correctional Services industry-sector to retain its workforce and manage and reduce attritional rates, while highlighting training opportunities.

content.badge: Workforce Strategies · Update on 2025 Workforce Strategies
leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia’s 2025 Correctional Services Workforce Plan, identified two challenges impacting the Correctional Services workforce:

paragraphs: Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report

blocks.title: Workforce Lifecycle
paragraphs: Challenge 1
Research and consultations indicated challenges across all stages of the workforce lifecycle contributing to increased workforce challenges.
bullets: Workforce attraction: Engagement indicated challenges to attracting a workforce that reflects the needs of the modern corrections environment.

Workforce recruitment: Existing recruitment challenges could influence how baseline requirements are modified to meet recruitment targets. Additionally, it was noted that the complexities of leave affect recruitment allocations, while regional facilities depend on either relocation funding or local recruitment which creates additional complexities. It was identified that recruitment practices for First Nations employees would benefit from a combination of cultural and role specific processes.

Onboarding: Pre-service training does not necessarily fully equip employees for the complexities of the physical and psychological demands of a Correctional Services role which may be driving retention challenges.

Retention: Limitations on learning and development opportunities, along with the mental health impacts (and increased psychological injury claims) in the industry-sector may be a contributing factor to retention.

blocks.title: First Nations Workforce Participation
paragraphs: Challenge 2

The high attrition of First Nations employees is a challenge for the Correctional Services industry-sector, with provision of formal cultural safety and wellbeing supports adding a further challenge in small and regional facilities due to financial limitations. Retention of First Nations employees is also a challenge in some organisations due to resource constraints, such as low attendance to optional cultural awareness or competency training due to employee resourcing limitations.

content.headerTitle: 1. Correctional Services Skills and Training Pathways (Workforce Lifecycle)
leadParagraphs: The 2025 Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report identified a strategy to review skills maintenance approaches throughout the workforce lifecycle. This was later retitled as the Correctional Services Skills and Training Pathways project and funded through activity project funding. The Correctional Services: Skills and Training Pathways Report was recommended to support Correctional Services through the development of comprehensive skills and training pathways in the industry-sector. Through consultation undertaken by Public Skills Australia for the 2025 Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report, it was noted that accredited training is mostly aligned to role progression, whereas non-accredited training is used variably in each jurisdiction and may be undertaken at the employee’s own direction in their own time. Further, resource constraints can impact the ability to provide diverse learning and professional development opportunities additional to any contractually mandated training.

It was recognised that training challenges may be contributing to ongoing workforce issues identified across the workforce lifecycle in the Correctional Services industry-sector. The intention of this project is to strengthen training and career pathways opportunities across the industry-sector.

paragraphs: Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report

blocks.title: This project aims to:
orderedList: 1 Map current occupational, career and training pathways within jurisdictions
2 Develop advice to strengthen occupational and educational pathways in Correctional Services
3 Identify opportunities for career progress into specialist operational roles to promote retention in the industry
4 Develop career outcomes and better training pathways to onboard, maintain and upskill Correctional Services employees
5 Identify areas of inconsistency in non-accredited training for future developments of the CSC Correctional Services Training Package.

paragraphs: This work will support several strategic priorities including:
This project will contribute to addressing Australia’s productivity challenges, including undertaking activity that supports building a skilled, adaptable and inclusive workforce.
Support industry-sectors to continue to build and maintain capable and mobile workforces that are future-ready.
Challenges to workforce productivity.

blocks.title: Project Progress Update

identify areas of non-accredited training that are used to bolster accredited courses
examine areas of potential update to the CSC Correctional Services Training Package.

leadParagraphs: A proposal to Investigate Barriers to First Nations Workforce Participation was put forward for further consideration in the 2025 Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report. This strategy proposal sought to investigate barriers for First Nations people to participate in the Correctional Services workforce, focussing on attraction, attrition and retention. Following the launch of the 2025 Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report, Public Skills Australia received a Statement of Federal Government priorities from the Minister for Employment and Workplace Relations and Minister for Skills and Training. This letter set out a priority to work with First Nations peoples, industry (employers and unions) across all Public Safety and Government industry-sectors and other JSCs to advance the priority reforms under the Closing the Gap National Agreement.

paragraphs: Correctional Services Workforce Insights Report

blocks.title: Project Progress Update
paragraphs: Noting this strategy proposal was scoped alongside the Statement of Federal Government priorities, Public Skills Australia has begun commissioning a research project through a First Nations-led research organisation on First Nations workforce participation across Public Safety and Government industry-sectors (including Correctional Services). This project will deliver a report (for each Public Safety and Government industry-sector) that seeks to collect and analyse statistical data on workforce participation of First Nations people broken down by age, gender, qualification enrolment and attainment over the past five years. The report will further collect qualitative data based on interviews and case studies, identifying personal stories of success working in the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors and resultant education and training journeys. This will seek to understand the challenges faced by, and the factors that impacted successful employment and/or aligned training for First Nations people.
