leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia's work is informed and guided by the Federal Government initiatives detailed below.

items.eyebrow: National Cabinet (Formerly Council of Australian Governments)
items.title: National Agreement on Closing the Gap (Closing the Gap)
summaryParagraphs: Closing the Gap is a commitment from all Australian governments and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander representatives to a fundamentally new way of developing and implementing policies and programs that impact the lives of First Nations people. This includes policies and programs impacting recruitment, health and social programs specific to First Nations peoples, which are relevant to the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors.

Closing the Gap is jointly implemented by the Federal, State and Territory governments, along with Australian Local Government Associations and Coalitions of Peaks. It focuses on four priority reforms (strengthen formal partnerships and shared decision making; build the community-controlled sector; transform government organisations; and shared access to data) and 19 national socio-economic targets, covering areas such as life expectancy, education, employment, justice and child protection. Overall progress towards meeting Closing the Gap targets has been mixed. Implementation of Closing the Gap is ongoing to 2031. The Productivity Commission is tracking these targets.

Closing the Gap performs a substantive role in informing Public Skills Australia’s research and engagement efforts. Closing the Gap informed consultation and engagement for the 2026 Corrections Workforce Insights Report. It will also inform the development and analysis of the proposed strategy Collaboration with HumanAbility to analyse recent updates to the CHC Community Services Training Package to identify contemporary practice that could inform future updates to the Community Corrections specialisations in the officers Certificate III and Certificate IV in Correctional Practice, when addressing the capability area of training for working with First Nations people.

items.eyebrow: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
items.title: The Australian Government’s Strategic Priorities
summaryParagraphs: The Federal Government’s strategic priorities provide a four-year (2022-2026) policy direction for the Australian Public Service (APS) and sets targets across key areas. These areas include the economy, public health and climate change.

The Australian Government’s Strategic Priorities are into the final year of their implementation by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet with the relevant APS departments and organisations. So far the Strategic Priorities, which have not been placed on set timelines, have achieved several outcomes, including hosting a Jobs and Skills Summit, developing a plan for cheaper child care, implementing fee-free Technical and Further Education (TAFE) and creating more university places, establishing the National Reconstruction Fund, introducing legislation for a national anti-corruption commission and strengthening strategic partnerships in the Pacific and South East Asia. Progress is still required for public health and aged care, improving housing supply and planning reforms and advancing government and budget sustainability.

The Australian Government’s Strategic Priorities focuses on TAFE accessibility, to reduce skills shortages across all industry-sectors in Australia. This will also be a significant factor in the proposed strategy Collaboration with HumanAbility to analyse recent updates to the CHC Community Services Training Package to identify contemporary practice that could inform future updates to the Community Corrections specialisations in the officers Certificate III and Certificate IV in Correctional Practice, which will look at addressing CCO skills requirements.

items.title: Working for Women – A Strategy for Gender Equality
summaryParagraphs: The Working for Women strategy outlines a framework for the Australian Government to improve national gender equality. It sets out five priority areas and reports on a range of outcomes and indicators annually to monitor Australia’s progress. These priority areas are:
Specific to JSCs, Priority Area 3 focuses on improving gender pay gaps, supporting access to skills and training and reducing occupational and industrial gender segregation.

To date, the Australian Government has increased female recruitment into trades and other occupations through apprenticeship support, fee-free TAFE and targets in the Australian Skills Guarantee, along with including gender equality as a national priority in the National Skills Agreement.

In March 2025, the DEWR launched the Advancing Gender Equality in Gender Segregated Industries grant program, directly linked to Priority Area 3. This grant program received a $28.5 million extension in December 2025.

Priority Area 3 of the Working for Women strategy – addressing economic equality and security – has informed the development of Public Skills Australia’s future work, in the proposed strategy Collaboration with HumanAbility to analyse recent updates to the CHC Community Services Training Package to identify contemporary practice that could inform future updates to the Community Corrections specialisations in the officers Certificate III and Certificate IV in Correctional Practice, which will consider priority cohorts in contemporary practices for community services, for the capabilities of future CCOs.
bullets: Priority Area 2 – Unpaid and paid care
Priority Area 3 – Economic equality and security
Priority Area 5 – Leadership, representation and decision making

items.title: The Clean Energy Generation: Workforce needs for a Net Zero Economy
summaryParagraphs: This series of reports considers emerging and future clean-energy workforce requirements as Australia strives to reach net-zero emissions by 2050. JSA’s preliminary modelling estimates Australia’s clean-energy workforce will need to grow from the current 53,000 employees to 84,000 employees by 2050.

The reports make 50 recommendations to support governments in focusing their efforts on how skills shortages can be averted in the set time, resources and legislative constraints and government objectives. Broadly, the recommendations cover the issue areas of participation and attraction, hiring and retention, transitioning employees and communities, roles and responsibilities, critical occupations, education and training and transport. Implementation remains ongoing and long-term, aligned with the 2050 net-zero target.

These reports provided contextual information for growing workforces in other industry-sectors within Public Skills Australia’s remit of Public Safety and Government. This provided insights into workforce pressures that may be felt by the Correctional Services industry-sector, due to modernising workforce needs and was considered for the 2026 Corrections Workforce Insights Report.

items.title: Australian Cyber Security Strategy
summaryParagraphs: The 2023-2030 Australian Cyber Security Strategy serves as a roadmap to achieve the Australian Government’s vision of becoming a world leader in cybersecurity by 2030.

The Strategy is structured around six ‘cyber shields’ (strong citizens and businesses, safe technology, world-class threat sharing, protected critical infrastructure, sovereign capability and resilient regional/global leadership). These are to be delivered in three stages or ‘Horizons’ (2023-2025 strengthening the foundations, 2026-2028 scaling efforts across the whole economy and 2029-2030 leading the development of new cyber technologies). Progress to date has been on the foundational aspects of the Strategy, with the initial work under ‘Horizon 1’ (2023-2025) concentrating on improving incident reporting and response mechanisms, introducing legislative reforms, piloting threat-sharing initiatives and raising government and critical infrastructure security standards. Overall coordination sits with the Department of Home Affairs, specifically through the Australian Cyber Security Coordinator. The remaining two horizons are to be implemented over the next four years up to 2030.

Cyber security was identified as a key theme during scoping for the proposed strategy Collaboration with HumanAbility to analyse recent updates to the CHC Community Services Training Package to identify contemporary practice that could inform future updates to the Community Corrections specialisations in the officers Certificate III and Certificate IV in Correctional Practice. New technologies and the cyber security risks they pose will be an ongoing consideration in Public Skills Australia’s engagement with the Correctional Services industry-sector.

items.title: Unlocking the Potential of VET
summaryParagraphs: In March 2024, the Qualification Reform Design Group (QRDG) provided advice to Skills Ministers on reforming the VET qualifications system. This included advising that:

As a result, Public Skills Australia undertook a Demonstration Project that consulted widely to determine the efficacy of updating qualification and unit of competency templates. This report was delivered to the QRDG in Q3 2024.

In December 2024, the QRDG provided their final report and recommendations to Skills Minsters, based on national consultation and findings from the JSC Demonstration Projects. The recommendations from this report centred around modernising VET qualifications by implementing a purpose-led, principles-based approach to qualification design. As a result, JSCs are responsible for ensuring qualifications serve a clear purpose, are linked to workforce needs and are not unnecessarily duplicated.

The advice from the ongoing QRDG work, directly informed the proposed strategy of Collaboration with HumanAbility to analyse recent updates to the CHC Community Services Training Package to identify contemporary practice that could inform future updates to the Community Corrections specialisations in the officers Certificate III and Certificate IV in Correctional Practice, as it will look to review and update the CHC Community Services Training Package.
bullets: Qualification and unit of competency design and development processes should be reviewed and updated where appropriate.
The VET system should be consolidated by removing training products that are under-utilised or unnecessarily duplicated.
The Training Package Organising Framework should be updated, where necessary.

items.title: Occupation Standard Classification for Australia
summaryParagraphs: Formerly known as the Australia New Zealand Standard Classification of Occupation (ANZSCO), the Occupation Standard Classification for Australia (OSCA) is a standardised framework for classifying occupations in Australia. As part of the replacement process from ANZSCO to OSCA in 2024, the ABS announced that OSCA will undergo regular updates in accordance with the OSCA Maintenance Strategy, which was released in 2025.

The changes to OSCA outlined in the Maintenance Strategy involve stakeholder engagement and are timed to ensure that each Census of Population and Housing uses the most recent update. Under the Strategy, the first round of consultations and feedback with stakeholders on proposed changes to OSCA are scheduled to be completed in August 2026, with the next update to be published in March 2027 before the data release of the 2026 Census in October 2027.

Public Skills Australia has in the 2026 Corrections Workforce Insights Report and will in future, where possible, utilise the most up-to-date version of OSCA to accurately report on occupational insights with whole-of-economy standards.

items.title: 2024 Core Skills Occupation List – Key Findings Report
summaryParagraphs: The Core Skills Occupation List (CSOL) provides labour market analysis that informs the identification of occupations that are considered appropriate for employer-sponsored temporary migration through the Core Skills Stream of the Skills in Demand (SID) Visa.

The 2024 CSOL Key Findings Report compiled a list of 456 occupations considered appropriate for the Core Skills Stream of the new employer-sponsored temporary SID visa. In addition to updating the list, JSA examined the drivers of skill shortages through CSOL analysis and stakeholder engagement and identified a ‘suitability gap’ category – occupations where there are enough qualified applicants, but they are not regarded as suitable by employers (e.g. auditors, electronics engineers, software and applications programmers). JSA also identified a ‘retention gap’ category – occupations with below-average rates of retention such as construction and hospitality jobs and child carers. JSA’s consultations to inform the 2025 CSOL opened in August 2025 and JSA submitted its advice to Government for consideration in October 2025.

The CSOL report provided contextual information for engagement and consultation of the 2026 Corrections Workforce Insights Report, in particular, insights into recruitment and retention for specific occupations.

items.title: Better Together – The Jobs and Skills Report 2024
summaryParagraphs: This report was released in November 2024 as part of JSA’s mandated obligations to provide insight on the Australian labour market and advice on workforce needs and priorities. This report details evidence aligned to five strategic pillars to enable a more prosperous economic future, including:

This report outlines JSA’s key current and emerging datasets that provide useful insights on the intricacies of Australia’s labour market for use in the development of strategic workforce planning for the JSCs.

The Better Together – The Jobs and Skills Report 2024, provided insight for the 2026 Corrections Workforce Insights Report for industry-sector engagement. Strategic pillar four, Optimising pathways and systems architecture, directly relates to the proposed strategy of Collaboration with HumanAbility to analyse recent updates to the CHC Community Services Training Package to identify contemporary practice that could inform future updates to the Community Corrections specialisations in the officers Certificate III and Certificate IV in Correctional Practice, as it proposes to review recent updates of the VET Training Packages for the Corrections industry-sector.
bullets: Fostering inclusive participation: Focused on broadening employment opportunities through identifying and removing barriers for people and communities.
Understanding today’s workforce: Detailing data to build an evidence base that informs and addresses current and emerging labour market and skills needs.
Shaping Australia’s future workforce: Projecting forward to plan for the opportunities and challenges of Australia’s future workforce needs.
Optimising pathways and system architecture: Monitoring, analysing and advising on the effectiveness of the VET system as key to skilling the workforce.

Activating an informed dialogue: Detailing stakeholder engagement across the VET system to provide the best evidence and advice on Australia’s current and future workforce and skills needs and opportunities.

items.title: Training Package Organising Framework
summaryParagraphs: In July 2025, the Training Package Organising Framework (TPOF) was updated based on advice from the QRDG in December 2024. Housing the Training Package Products Development and Endorsement Process Policy (TPPDEPP), Training Package Products Policy (TPPP) and the Standards for Training Packages, the TPOF sets out the process for developing and seeking approval of new VET training products for JSCs. As a JSC, Public Skills Australia will continue to adhere to the TPOF to ensure the Australian VET system is high-performing and readily supports student and industry needs.

The updated TPOF provides specific guidance to all projects that may result in changes to any training products. This includes the 2026 Corrections Workforce Insights Report, where the TPOF provides guidance on best practice development and approval of VET training products for proposed strategies, such as Collaboration with HumanAbility to analyse recent updates to the CHC Community Services Training Package to identify contemporary practice that could inform future updates to the Community Corrections specialisations in the officers Certificate III and Certificate IV in Correctional Practice.

items.title: Opportunity and Productivity: Towards a Tertiary Harmonisation Roadmap Report
summaryParagraphs: This report seeks to articulate the benefits of a more harmonised tertiary sector and provides recommendations on how to create a sustainable pathway forward in collaboration with key stakeholders. It outlines 19 key recommendations, across three categories (enabling the tertiary harmonisation roadmap, early priorities for the roadmap and medium-term horizon roadmap priorities) to work towards a harmonised system that can tackle national challenges, address skilled workforce shortages and improve productivity.

The report has provided insightful recommendations which have been utilised in stakeholder engagement for the development of the proposed project, Collaboration with HumanAbility to analyse recent updates to the CHC Community Services Training Package to identify contemporary practice that could inform future updates to the Community Corrections specialisations in the officers Certificate III and Certificate IV in Correctional Practice, which aims at addressing skilled workforce shortages in community corrections services through the analysis of recent training package updates.

items.title: Gender Economic Equality Study
summaryParagraphs: The Gender Economic Equality Study explored three challenges for the jobs and skills systems that contribute to gender economic inequality:

The study was reported over three papers, with the third and final paper Speeding up progress towards gender economic equality being released in October 2025. This paper sets out 10 recommendations to address challenges in the jobs and skills system that perpetuate inequality and impact productivity:

The recommendations of the paper have provided strategic and important goals for Public Skills Australia to work toward, and have been influential in projects undertaken in 2025-2026, such as the Workforce Lifecycle Project, by providing context on priority cohorts to improve gender equality across the jobs and skills systems.
bullets: pay gaps and gendered divides in education

items.title: Occupational Shortage List
summaryParagraphs: The Occupational Shortage List (OSL), which was formerly the Skills Priority List, offers an annual point-in-time review of the status of Australian occupations. Specifically, the OSL reports on whether occupations (at the 4-digit and 6-digit ANZSCO level and the 6-digit OSCA level) are experiencing shortages nationally and for each State and Territory in regional or metropolitan areas.

The OSL was last updated in 2025. The latest list differed from previous iterations due to the fact that in 2024 the ANZSCO classification framework for occupations was replaced with the OSCA framework. In terms of the 2025 OSL results, it was reported that 29 per cent of occupations (293 out of 1022 assessed) were in national shortage, which was 4 per cent lower than 2024 (33 per cent) and more than 7 per cent lower than 2023 (36 per cent). The OSL in 2025 also added 29 occupations newly in shortage compared to 2024, most of which were roles related to health, science, technicians and trades and machinery operators and drivers. As at February 2026, JSA had started the 2026 OSL survey but it had not yet confirmed a publication date for this year’s list.

The OSL provided important context for stakeholder consultation preparation for the 2026 Corrections Workforce Insights Report. This list indicates, on a national level, where specific occupation gaps currently exist and enabled Public Skills Australia to pursue engagements with Correctional Services stakeholders on whether these demands exist within their contexts.

leadParagraphs: The 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report (the Report) is the fourth report generated by Public Skills Australia for the Public Safety industry-sectors since 2023.[[2]] It builds on the previous iterations to identify workforce challenges and strategic initiatives to mitigate them. leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia is the Jobs and Skills Council (JSC) for the Public Safety and Government industry, comprising Correctional Services, Defence, Federal, State/Territory and Local Government, Fire and Emergency Services and Police industry-sectors.

Through its work, Public Skills Australia actively supports employer and employee bodies in these industries and associated volunteer associations. Public Skills Australia works in partnership with the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR) and other JSCs to give effect to broader Ministerial and government priorities.

blocks.title: Our commitment
paragraphs: Public Skills Australia remains committed to encouraging the participation of First Nations people,[[1]] those from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, those living with or experiencing disabilities, women and other gender diverse people and mature people in the Public Safety and Government industry workforces.

[[1]] Please note, First Nations people will be used as preferred terminology inclusive of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders. When citing a data source (such as government strategies or state of the sector reports) the terminology of the data source will be used to maintain accurate data representation.

leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia's Workforce Insights Reports are developed using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data obtained from primary and secondary sources. This 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report is supported by data obtained through stakeholder consultations and engagements.

These consultations were used to gain insight into challenges each industry-sector is facing with the development and maintenance of a skilled workforce. The challenges identified through consultations were thematically analysed to identify trends and priority areas to address for each industry-sector. Following these consultations, Public Skills Australia conducted secondary qualitative and quantitative research to verify the challenges raised. Additional targeted consultations with senior stakeholders were held to further validate workforce challenges and identify related industry insights. Specific to the Public Safety industry-sectors, and in alignment with the tripartite approach for Jobs and Skills Councils (JSCs), consultations were held with employers, employee bodies and Government organisations, both in-person and through online meetings, workshops and presentations. Drafts were subsequently progressed through Public Skills Australia's governance process that includes:

Public Skills Australia thanks the contributors, including industry representatives, its Board and governance group representatives, the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR) and Jobs and Skills Australia (JSA) for sharing their views and data generously, and supporting the development of this Report.

blocks.title: 1 · Public Safety Subcommittee
paragraphs: The Subcommittee is responsible for recommending this report to the Industry Advisory Group (IAG) for endorsement.
This recommendation is made on the basis that the Subcommittee is satisfied that sufficient consultation and engagement has been undertaken, and that consultation feedback was appropriately actioned.

blocks.title: 2 · Industry Advisory Group
paragraphs: The IAG is responsible for endorsing this report to the Public Skills Australia Board for approval to be submitted to DEWR.

This endorsement is made on the basis that the IAG is satisfied with the Public Safety Subcommittee's recommendation for endorsement. The IAG further provides its strategic guidance and endorsement if comfortable that the strategic priorities of Public Safety and Government industry-sectors are also captured.

blocks.title: 3 · Public Skills Australia Board
paragraphs: The Public Skills Australia Board (the Board) is responsible to approve the submission of the report to DEWR.

This approval is made on the basis that the Board is satisfied that an appropriate development and consultation process was followed and that the report has been progressed in line with the internal governance requirements of Public Skills Australia.

The report uses publicly available datasets accessible from Jobs and Skills Australia (JSA), the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS), the National Centre for Vocational Education Research (NCVER) and other supporting online sources. Due to the complexity of large-scale workforce data, no single source provides an accurate or complete picture. Therefore, multiple data sources are used to provide the most accurate representation of the workforce as possible, supported by qualitative research (including interviews with stakeholders). This report prioritises the data source, or combination of data sources, that provide the most accurate representation of the workforce possible. This research was bolstered by literature reviews of government reports and documents, online sources, annual reports, departmental documentation, legislation, research articles and relevant Royal Commission Reports.

leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia’s 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report considers the wider operational contexts impacting Public Safety and Government industry-sectors. It identifies four drivers of change that will impact workforce planning in the short to medium term, aligned with the nine megatrends detailed in previous Workforce Insights Reports, that remain relevant to long term workforce trends.

The Report analyses themes consistent across all three Public Safety industry-sectors before examining each Public Safety industry-sector individually. The report provides data analysis, identifying workforce insights and detailing strategies aimed at addressing workforce challenges.

blocks.title: Public Safety Workforce Themes & Insights Across Sectors

items.title: Challenges in rapid adoption of emerging technology remains, due to significant security screening requirements for any new technology adoption. Limitations exist for the speed of being able to upskill employees in the use of any new technology.

Provisioning targeted training faster through short courses (often referred to as micro-credentials). Leveraging Vocational Education and Training Units of Competency could be effective in responding to emerging technologies.
The Vocational Education and Training (VET) system remains important for the ADF as it provides a national standard, with meaningful qualifications written by industry, for industry.

Greater focus is required to support those transitioning (including veterans) to articulate the transferability of their VET qualifications and the relevance of their ADF experience to the civilian workforce. Where support is available, the information provided could be bolstered.

Specialist disaster recovery functions are operationally focused, a more contemporary approach now requires capabilities related to the unique aspects of working with communities that may be grieving or socially, emotionally and financially impacted.

Challenges in access to nationally accredited disaster recovery training products leads to inconsistencies in recovery outcomes, reduced community trust and limits the ability of communities to rebuild from the impacts of disasters.

Australia is experiencing a critical challenge in maintaining capability to use fire effectively in the landscape, particularly for complex prescribed burning and backburning during bushfire suppression.
The HLTAID010 unit of competency is an entry-level first aid training product that is no longer meeting the operational needs for volunteer surf lifesavers.

Incidents involving hazardous materials are becoming increasingly important while current training may be limiting in some Fire and Emergency Services organisations ability to deliver this type of service.
Skills shortages and strong demand for similar skills may require the establishment of multiple entry pathways for digital forensic professionals into policing.

The VET system is well established to deliver a nationally consistent approach to training, however, the Police Training Package currently does not contain a qualification specialising in digital forensics.

Police officers being required to take on more leadership responsibilities earlier in their careers, particularly in regional, rural and remote areas, where workforce shortages are more pronounced. This may require more support in accelerating leadership skills development.

subSections.title: Driver 1 — Resilience of organisations to respond to strategic shocks
paragraphs: Organisational resilience is emerging as a critical driver of change across Australia’s Public Safety and Government industry-sectors, particularly as agencies confront increasingly frequent and complex strategic shocks. Recent experience with compounding crises (such as increasingly intense bushfires, major cyber attacks and intensifying geopolitical tensions) have exposed structural vulnerabilities and highlighted the need for more adaptive, anticipatory and integrated capabilities. Investment will be required to deepen organisational capabilities that supports system-wide preparedness, robust governance and the ability to maintain critical functions under stress.[[3]]

blocks.title: Driver 2 — Challenges to workforce productivity
paragraphs: In its Five Pillars of Productivity enquiry reports, the Productivity Commission observed that productivity growth has been slowing globally since the mid-2000s, with Australia experiencing the slowest productivity growth in 60 years. The Productivity Commission identified long-standing pressures that have contributed to the productivity slowdown, including market stagnation, a persistently tight labour market and slower uptake of technological innovations.[[4]]
These factors are further exacerbated by emerging challenges linked to the megatrends including an ageing population, technological development, climate change and competition for labour.[[5]]

blocks.title: Driver 3 — Emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), greater automation and broader digital transformation
paragraphs: AI, automation and accelerated digital transformation are powerful drivers of organisational and system-level change in the short term. This is reinforced by a push from the Federal Government for greater adoption of AI and digital initiatives across federal agencies.[[6]]

These initiatives signal a shift toward embedding AI into core service delivery, regulatory functions and operational decision making. AI, automation and digital transformation represent an opportunity for significant capability uplift through AI-enabled analytics, automation of high-volume processes and advanced digital platforms that enhance situational awareness, threat detection and emergency response coordination. Conversely, they represent a growing security risk as they are also being leveraged by threat actors to disrupt government services, facilitate foreign interference, enable disinformation, promote false narratives through deepfakes and erode trust in government institutions.[[7]]

This is important as these drivers of change will likely impact the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors in the short to medium term.

blocks.title: Driver 4 — Workforce inclusivity
paragraphs: Workforce inclusivity has been a key focus across the labour market. In the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors this is likely to translate into a continued focus on recruiting, retaining and developing employees from diverse cultural, linguistic, gender, disability and neurodivergent backgrounds. As organisations seek to increase workforce participation from these cohorts, they will be required to adapt and change legacy systems and processes to respond to the needs of the modern workforce.

leadParagraphs: Public Safety industry-sectors are responsible for safeguarding Australia’s people, property and environment through the combined efforts of the Defence, Fire and Emergency Services and Police industry-sectors. These industry-sectors prepare for, respond to and recover from natural disasters, emergency incidents, law and order, sovereign capabilities and geopolitical uncertainty.

In addition to the themes above, Public Safety industry-sectors are increasingly required to improve cross-sector interoperability allowing organisations to interact, balance different legal arrangements and provide surge capacity. This requires a level of cross-industry skills recognition.

Greater cross-industry skills recognition of transferable competencies is essential for sustainable interoperability. When personnel from Defence, Fire and Emergency Services and Police share a common understanding of incident-management language, technical skills (communications, logistics, command and control) and recognised qualifications, multi-organisation teams can integrate faster, reduce safety risks and maintain surge capability during prolonged or simultaneous operations.

items.title: Public Safety’s regulatory environment
summaryParagraphs: Public Safety industry-sectors are institutions  accountable to governments. As such, they are  subject to regulatory oversight bodies, government  fiscal positions (including budget constraints  and financial accountability) and are impacted by  election cycles and political commitments.

items.title: Public Safety taskings
summaryParagraphs: The Public Safety workforce is required to remain  agile and responsive to urgent taskings. This  requires that Public Safety organisations ensure  they are prepared to ‘scale up’ workforce resources  in response to natural disasters, emergency  incidents, geopolitical events etc, through  leveraging available surge capacity.

items.title: Public Safety’s resourcing
summaryParagraphs: The Public Safety workforce uses a mix of career  uniform personnel, reservists, volunteers and public sector personnel, to be fit for purpose across various contexts.

items.title: Public Safety’s risk environment
summaryParagraphs: The Public Safety workforce is exposed to  demanding and, at times, hazardous work  conditions. These workforces are trained to operate  within high-stress and challenging environments  but are not immune to resultant injury. This is a  significant factor affecting workforce sustainability.

leadParagraphs: VET training products can be leveraged to potentially reduce duplication of training package development, training material development and support skill recognition in and between the Public Safety industry-sectors (impacting workforce mobility, interoperability, career transition and enhancing productivity).
When shared skills, such as those identified in the Specialist Skills Alignment section, are recognised and aligned, it may enable smoother integration of personnel in joint operations environments.

Some areas in Public Safety industry-sectors further seek to use recognition of prior learning (RPL) to reduce lead in times for personnel transitioning. Noting the similarity of operational context and skills, this may be further leveraged and give effect to important recommendations such as the Recommendation 83 of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide.

blocks.title: Challenges in the delivery of Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) services
paragraphs: The Productivity Commission identified the following challenges in the delivery of RPL services.[[11]] This includes:

subSections.title: Challenges with RPL fraud
paragraphs: The prevalence of RPL fraud makes acceptance of RPL in the VET sector complicated, resulting in a loss of trust in the RPL process. In turn, this means that personnel often are required to complete training for a unit of competency that they already hold, resulting in productivity losses and more impost on already strained training services in the Public Safety industry-sectors. The Productivity Commission indicated that fewer than 5 per cent of successful completions/results are granted through RPL. Further, as the VET sector is highly regulated by quality assurance organisations such as the Training Accreditation Council (TAC – Western Australia), Victoria Registration Qualifications Authority (VRQA – Victoria) and the Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA – for the remainder of the states and territories), Registered Training Organisations (RTOs), TAFEs and employers are reluctant to accept RPL outcomes due to the evidence required of competency by documents such as the ASQA 2025 Standards for RTOs. This is loosely referred to as ‘audit fear’, dissuading genuine training providers from using RPL and/or underreporting its use.

subSections.title: RPL processes are costly and complex
paragraphs: RPL applications require the same rigour of assessment as when assessing a student’s competency for the first time. Extensive portfolios of evidence are required, often resulting in students requested to either repeat training or undertaking vigorous assessments to ‘prove’ competence. Further, RPL requires assessors familiar and experience in RPL, which make RPL assessments costly (both timing and financial costs).

However, it is exactly this contextualisation of training that limits RPL when employees want to work in other industries.

blocks.title: Emerging technologies across the labour market
paragraphs: Theme One, Insight One

Challenges in rapid adoption of emerging technology remain, due to significant security screening requirements for any new technology adoption. Limitations on how rapidly upskilling in the use of any new technology also remains.

Across the broader labour market in Australia, emerging technologies are considered to be drivers of long-term productivity growth. Adopting these emerging technologies requires supporting workforces to rapidly train and upskill, changing traditional approaches to training.[[16]] It is anticipated that across the labour market, Australia will require 1.3 million technology professionals by 2030, equating to 52,000 employees.[[17]] Recent data indicates that between 2016 and 2021, 75,000 Information and Communication Technology (ICT) students entered the broader technology sector following completion of a university or VET qualification, which equates to only 15,000 ICT professionals annually.[[18]]

While not Defence-specific, this shortage indicates the need to ensure the ADF workforce is not only appropriately skilled to deploy emerging technologies, but that individuals are attracted and retained, noting the competing need for such professionals across the wider labour market.

The adoption of the 2024 National Defence Strategy has resulted in a change in capability priorities for the ADF, which has now moved “to an integrated, focused force designed to address Australia's most significant strategic risks”. This is markedly different from the previous balanced force approach, which was structured to respond to a range of possibilities.[[19]] Noting this change, ADF stakeholders who were consulted, emphasised the importance of training for capability that is agile and resilient to strategic shocks, and adaptable to government priorities.

blocks.title: Capability investment priorities
paragraphs: Theme One, Insight Two

Provisioning targeted training faster through short courses (often referred to as micro-credentials ) leveraging Vocational Education and Training Units of Competency could be effective in responding to emerging technologies.

Recruitment, training and retention of a highly specialised and skilled workforce is necessary to meet emerging technology challenges and future capability needs.[[20]] As detailed in the Industry Overview section, the ADF workforce has been expanding in recent years due to an increase in enlistments alongside a decline in separations. Defence stakeholders noted that the ADF workforce will need to enhance their ability to upskill this workforce to be technically proficient in new and emerging technologies.[[21]]
The 2024 Integrated Investment Program outlines $330 billion through to 2033-34 on capability investment priorities that include the following areas (relating to new and emerging technologies):[[22]]

As a result of the need to acquire emerging technologies to be able to respond to future threats, the ADF faces the challenge of ensuring that their personnel can rapidly acquire and refresh highly technical skills (at pace with operational needs), while continuing to meet current job role requirements in increasingly complex and dangerous environments.

Defence stakeholders and public announcements by the Federal Government have consistently identified uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS-drone) as a critical technology where more training will support operational needs.[[23]] At an international level, it is acknowledged that UAS technology and counter-drone systems are evolving at a much faster rate than traditional acquisition and training cycles (in large part due to their evolving use in the war in Ukraine). Ukraine has developed and invested in counter-drone systems that are built to efficiently respond to threats that never previously existed.[[24]] The fast innovation of the Ukraine in response to these threats has been used in NATO training exercises, and provides an example of the way that the ADF could adapt to future threats, with drone technology evolving “every two to three weeks [with a] fundamentally different [model].”[[25]] The Australian Government has made a $10 billion commitment to UAS over the next 10 years from 2025 that includes:

In Australia, initiatives such as the Remotely Piloted Aircraft Training School (RPATS) have been established, with Australian Air Force Cadets now eligible for Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) training to qualify as fully certified drone pilots.[[27]] Additional training for drone capability and other emerging technologies is currently available through programs such as the National Security TAFE Centre of Excellence.[[28]] However, through consultations, Defence stakeholders advised that the current available training in the AVI Aviation Training Package is generic, and that Defence-specific training will likely be required to align to varying job roles in the ADF.

Theme Two, Insight One
The Vocational Education and Training (VET) system remains important for the ADF as it provides a national standard, with meaningful qualifications written by industry, for industry.

The Final Report for the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide details the transition from military to civilian life and examines the challenges that veterans may face when seeking employment post-service.[[30]]

Of the 122 recommendations, Recommendation 83: “Increase opportunities for personnel to gain civilian qualifications from Defence training and education, Focus Area C ‘fill the gap’ between Defence and civilian training (where an equivalent civilian qualification exists), either by expanding the content of the Defence training course or by funding bridging training for personnel prior to separation” was highlighted in the 2025 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report as a focus area for Public Skills Australia to support the Defence industry-sector.[[31]]

The skills and experience that ADF personnel obtain throughout their service can be considered towards any additional study post-service, or towards future job roles in the civilian workforce through RPL provided by ADF Transition and Civil Recognition.[[32]] Once assessed, a veteran’s existing skills, work level standards and experience can result in being awarded qualifications and/or micro-credentials which have transferability to industries external to Defence.[[33]]

Defence stakeholders emphasised the importance of the VET system for this purpose as associated education and training products represents particular skills (through the units of competency) as a national standard for relevant occupations.[[34]] Awarding VET qualifications allows Defence veterans to demonstrate that they have met a national standard that can be recognised across the country by RTOs, industries and employers.[[35]]

blocks.title: Articulating skills — state and territory support
paragraphs: Theme Two, Insight Two

Greater focus is required to support those transitioning (including veterans) to articulate the transferability of their VET qualifications and the relevance of their ADF experience to the civilian workforce. Where support is available, the information provided could be bolstered.

While much of the focus for transitioning veterans was based on issuing VET qualifications post-service, a challenge raised by Defence stakeholders related to enabling veterans to articulate their skills through their VET qualifications to prospective employers. Current support for veterans to articulate their skills is available, however the programs and information differ based on states and territories.

Defence stakeholders advised that the current support should be bolstered – Appendix A – Defence Veterans’ Programs and Initiatives – highlights some of the programs in each state and territory, and the information available to support veteran transition out of the ADF and into the civilian workforce.

Some programs, such as TAFE NSW Ranks to Recognition Program, mirror the ADF programs offered to transitioning and transitioned veterans. Additionally, some states and territories (such as the Northern Territory) have adopted initiatives like the Rank to Grade Guide to better support veterans.[[36]] In the ACT, the ACTPS Veterans’ Employment Strategy has not been updated since 2020 but rather aligned to the broader programs at the federal level.

Defence stakeholders emphasised that transitioning veterans should be provided with clear information to understand how the qualifications they obtained during service is relevant in the civilian workforce. This may be further supported through guidance on the programs on offer, options available and understanding how the varying roles and ranks across the ADF could translate to a civilian context. An additional benefit could be the identification of where such services could be streamlined.
Industry Insight
The Vocational Education and Training (VET) system remains important for the ADF as it provides a national standard, with meaningful qualifications written by industry, for industry.

leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia proposes the following strategies aligned to the workforce insights identified to support Defence:

items.title: Support Defence skill and capability requirements to operationalise drones
items.objective: Map current Defence micro-credentials on drones and unmanned aerial systems (UAS) to existing units of competency from current VET qualifications.
approach: Identify whether current units of competency relating to UAS and drones meet the skills requirements of Defence. Should gaps be found, review/develop new units of competency to address these gaps.
items.impact: Support the Defence workforce by enabling rapid, targeted upskilling in UAS and drone related technologies.
stakeholders: Defence Education, Learning and Training Authority (DELTA)

items.title: Support transition of Defence Veterans to civilian workforce
items.objective: Support Recommendation 83(c) of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide by supporting up-to-date information facilitated by state and territory initiatives that assist transitioning veterans.
approach: Collaborate with Defence to map ADF job roles and training to the Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) levels and approximate equivalent civilian qualifications.
Develop material that translates military terminology into civilian contexts, to build collective understanding for both transitioning veterans and prospective civilian employers.
Collaborate with Defence to share this information back through state and territories to be included on their websites for veterans.
items.impact: Support Recommendation 83(c) by providing information through Defence, states and territories that support veterans to translate their Defence skills and experience into civilian-recognised language.
stakeholders: Defence Education, Learning and Training Authority (DELTA)

items.title: Australian Government National Defence: Defence Strategic Review
summaryParagraphs: The National Defence: Defence Strategic Review 2023 outlined recommended reforms to Defence’s posture and structure. The review provides 62 recommendations across a range of strategic focus areas, including but not limited to workforce, capability, technology, resourcing and logistics. This strategic review preceded the development of the 2024 National Defence Strategy and update of the Integrated Investment Program 2024. It recommended a biennial strategic update through a National Defence Strategy, with the 2024 National Defence Strategy the first iteration of the strategic update. The Defence Strategic Review notes that it should be considered in conjunction with the 2024 National Defence Strategy and the Integrated Investment Program 2024.

Initial progress on a range of other recommendation focus areas is described at the Australian Government Transparency Portal.41 Continued progress against the recommendations is also documented in the Defence Annual Report 2024–25.42

detailSections.heading: Consultation and engagement
paragraphs: Considered in conjunction with the National Defence Strategy 2024 and the Integrated Investment Plan 2024, which provided detail and context for engagements and consultations.

detailSections.heading: 2025 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: Informed the development of Workforce Strategies identified in the National Defence Strategy 2024 and the Integrated Investment Program 2024. Together they provide the framework for Public Skills Australia’s Defence projects.

detailSections.heading: 2026 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: Will provide context and data for the development of initial research for the Support Defence skill and capability requirements to operationalise drones project.

items.title: Australian Government National Defence Strategy 2024
summaryParagraphs: The National Defence Strategy outlines the Government’s approach to Australia’s National Defence risks. Six priorities are highlighted in the strategy including:
An update to the National Defence Strategy is due to be delivered by the Department of Defence in 2026.
bullets: Acquisition of nuclear-powered submarines through AUKUS
Improving the growth and retention of the workforce
Lifting Australia’s capacity to rapidly translate disruptive new technologies into ADF capability

detailSections.heading: Consultation and engagement
paragraphs: Provided context on Defence’s forward strategy, specifically the strategy of deterrence and denial, that informs force design and acquisition priorities that informed consultations with Defence stakeholders.

detailSections.heading: 2025 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: Informed the development of:

Specifically, the National Defence Strategy 2024 identified both space and cyber skills as key components of Defence’s Capability Investment Priorities. Additionally, Training and skilling reform was identified as part of the wider Defence reform agenda, which directly informed the design and agenda for the VET System Pathways Framework.

detailSections.heading: 2026 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: Support Defence skill and capability requirements to operationalise drones and its focus on UAS and drones will be informed by the Capability Investment Priorities: Priorities for the integrated, focused force section of the strategy.
Support transition of Defence Veterans to civilian workforce will be informed by the insights of the People: Culture section of this strategy.

items.title: Australian Government 2024 Defence Workforce Plan
summaryParagraphs: The 2024 Defence Workforce Plan outlines Australia’s strategy to expand and enhance the ADF and APS workforce, aiming to grow the permanent ADF workforce to 69,000 by the early 2030s and the combined ADF and APS workforce to around 100,000 by 2040. Key initiatives include extending the Continuation Bonus, increasing Operational Reserves, improving mental health support and aligning workforce growth with capability needs across various domains. The plan also emphasises cultural improvements and significant financial investments, with $5.7 billion allocated over the next four years and $50.3 billion over the next decade.

Since its release Defence has recorded the largest recruitment surge for the ADF in August 2025. Additionally in February 2026 new roles in the Space domain were announced for direct entry into the ADF.

detailSections.heading: Consultation and engagement
paragraphs: Provided context on workforce priorities in consultations with Defence stakeholders and set clear workforce planning expectations.

detailSections.heading: 2025 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: The VET System Pathways Framework was informed by Strategic Task 5 – Development and Transformation of the Defence Workforce, which identified Defence education and training as core components of workforce attraction and enhancement.

Both space and cyber capabilities are identified in Chapter 2: Delivering an Integrated, Focused Force (point 2.17) as critical skillsets pivotal to Defence’s situational awareness and warfighting capabilities.

detailSections.heading: 2026 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: Support transition of Defence Veterans to civilian workforce will be informed by Strategic Task 8: Support to Defence Personnel, ADF Families and Transitioning Personnel.

items.title: Australian Government Defence Industry Development Strategy
summaryParagraphs: The Defence Industry Development Strategy outlines Australia’s plan to build a sovereign Defence industrial base to enhance national security and military preparedness. It emphasises the need for a robust industrial structure, identifies seven Sovereign Defence Industrial Priorities (SDIPs) and details initiatives for industry growth, workforce development, innovation and exports. The strategy also highlights the importance of security measures to protect sensitive technologies and information.
Since its release there have been several announcements for initiatives that support the SDIPs including:
bullets: A total $30 billion investment in the Osborne Shipyard in South Australia to support construction of the AUKUS submarines
$17 million has been allocated to 44 Australian businesses in the latest rounds of the Defence Industry Development Grants (DIDG) program in January 2026
$1.4 billion to advance collaborative air capabilities through the MQ-28A Ghost Bat
Beginning of production for Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System (GMLRS) missiles in December 2025 at a new factory in Port Wakefield, South Australia.

detailSections.heading: Consultation and engagement
paragraphs: Provided context on sovereign capability priorities in consultations with Defence stakeholders.

detailSections.heading: 2025 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: Chapter 8 – Workforce of the strategy described building a skilled and capable workforce as being at the core of Defence’s efforts to modernise its capabilities and informed the development of the VET System Pathways Framework.

detailSections.heading: 2026 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: Support Defence skill and capability requirements to operationalise drones will be informed by Sovereign Defence Industrial Priority 5: Development and integration of autonomous systems.

items.title: Australian Government Integrated Investment Program
summaryParagraphs: The Integrated Investment Program outlines the Defence capability investment priorities, including, but not limited to: Undersea Warfare, Maritime capabilities, Space and Cyber, Targeting and Long-Range Strike and Missile Defence. The Integrated Investment Program includes developing a skilled workforce in identified investment areas.

Since the release of this Strategy, the Minister of Defence announced in December 2025 the establishment of the Defence Delivery Agency. This new agency will integrate three existing capability delivery groups:
The aim of this agency is aimed at enabling coordinated and holistic delivery of defence capability and growing sovereign defence industrial base.
bullets: Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance Group

detailSections.heading: Consultation and engagement
paragraphs: Provided context on capability acquisition priorities and the skills requirements to deploy them in consultations with Defence stakeholders.

detailSections.heading: 2025 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: Informed the development of:

Chapter 1: Investing in the National Defence Strategy outlined that investing in a highly skilled workforce is critical to successfully achieving its workforce strategy. This includes “skilling initiatives” related to growing and attracting the required workforce which informed all three strategies.

Additionally, Chapter 6: Space and Cyber is dedicated to describing Defence’s investment commitment to enhancing its capabilities in both areas and provided foundational work for Public Skills Australia’s strategies in this area.

detailSections.heading: 2026 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: Support Defence skill and capability requirements to operationalise drones and its focus on UAS and drones will be informed by the Chapter 8: Expeditionary Air Operations: Uncrewed air systems investment area.

items.title: Australian Government Response to the Final Report of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide
summaryParagraphs: The Australian Government Response to the Final Report of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide commits to addressing systemic challenges and risk factors related to suicide among current and former ADF personnel, agreeing to most of the Royal Commission’s 122 recommendations.

Specific to Public Skills Australia, Recommendation 83 describes the requirement for Defence “to increase opportunities for members to gain civilian qualifications from Defence training and education.”
The Reform Management Plan was approved by the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide Implementation Program Board on 12 December 2025.

In December 2025 it was announced that 32 recommendations will be implemented by the end of 2025, with work underway on the remainder of the recommendation. For initiatives across Defence and State/Territory governments in support of Veterans transitioning out of defence careers refer Appendix A.

detailSections.heading: Consultation and engagement
paragraphs: This document outlines critical priorities for Defence and provided substantial material and recommendations to consult on through Defence engagements.

detailSections.heading: 2025 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: Informed the:
Specifically, both the VET System Pathways Framework and Scoping Proposal were guided by Recommendation 83(c) that describes the need for expansion of Defence’s education and training programs.

completion of Scoping Proposal to Investigate the Development of Pathways for Transitioning Veterans

detailSections.heading: 2026 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: This report will inform Public Skills Australia’s research into Support transition of Defence Veterans to civilian workforce, which proposes to increase opportunities for ADF members to gain civilian qualifications by expanding existing Defence training courses.

summaryParagraphs: This plan sets out the activities required to uplift the ADF’s maritime capability. This includes enabling:
Importantly, this plan describes Australia’s commitment to continuous naval shipbuilding and sustainment.
In February 2027 the Prime Minister announced a total $30 billion investment in the Osborne Shipyard in South Australia to support construction of the AUKUS submarines.

detailSections.heading: Consultation and engagement
paragraphs: Provided guidance on priorities for enabling the AUKUS work program in consultations with Jobs and Skills Australia, the Australian Submarine Organisation and Defence stakeholders.

detailSections.heading: 2025 Workforce Strategies
paragraphs: Informed the development of the Defence Capability – VET System Pathways Framework Project. Specifically, Chapter 3: Workforce identifies the need for the Vocational Education and Training system to support the upskilling of Defence’s shipbuilding and submarine workforce.

summaryParagraphs: The Defence Digital Strategy and Roadmap document provides comprehensive guidance on Defence’s plan to stay well positioned in the digital age. This strategy sets out the following three priorities:
Collectively, this strategy ensures Defence enhances its ICT capabilities to deliver critical digital functions.

Specifically, the strategy describes ICT capabilities as being at the core of its commitment to becoming a “best-in-class workforce”, maintaining “best-in-class global platforms” and possessing “best-in-class sovereign capabilities”.

items.title: ACT Government Veterans’ Employment Strategy, 2020
summaryParagraphs: Articulates the benefits of both the private and public sectors as career pathways for veterans and their families and highlights the resources available (at the time of publishing) for recruitment, networking and information sharing.[[87]]

items.title: ACT Public Service (ACTPS) Veterans’ Employment Transition Guide, 2018
summaryParagraphs: Provides ADF personnel with guidance on how their skills and experience can be translated into the ACTPS. Provides information on the ACTPS as an employer, as well as tips on identifying the right role and understanding the lifecycle of the application process.[[88]]

items.title: ADF Transition and Civil Recognition Project
summaryParagraphs: Provides transitioning personnel, and those who have transitioned in 24 months, the opportunity to have skills recognised through RPL, and accredited training where possible.[[89]]

items.title: ADF Transition Guide App, 2024
summaryParagraphs: Provides a free App to ADF personnel, their families and support networks to understand and navigate the transition into civilian life. Provides the most current transition information from across Defence to assist personnel in preparing for their transition out of the ADF.[[90]]

items.title: The ADF Personnel and Family Transition Guide (2024-25)
summaryParagraphs: Provides personnel and their families with information about the transition process and supports available, and informs what is provided in the ADF Transition Guide App.[[91]]

items.title: ADF Transition Training & Skills Guide
summaryParagraphs: Provides explanation to personnel across the ADF of the skills acquired during their service and general guidance on how this can apply to the civilian workforce. Guides are grouped by the equivalent military rank from each service area – Navy, Army and Air Force.[[92]]

items.title: Department of Premier and Cabinet Tasmania, Tasmanian Veterans’ Employment Strategy 2023-2027
summaryParagraphs: Sets out a range of supports and employment opportunities available for veterans in Tasmania and is designed to complement initiatives already underway at a national level. Provides case studies of veterans who have successfully transitioned to a civilian career, now working in the Tasmanian State Service.[[93]]

items.title: Department of Veterans’ Affairs Veteran Transition Strategy (2023) and Action Plan (2024)
summaryParagraphs: Identifies six priority areas that are intended to support a positive transition out of the ADF. The Veteran Transition Action Plan provides the actions to support the implementation of the six priority areas identified in the Strategy, detailing the actions to be undertaken and the responsible organisation.[[94]][[95]]

items.title: Department of Veterans’ Affairs Veteran Employment Program
summaryParagraphs: Delivers initiatives to support employers in improving employment outcomes for ADF veterans. Organisations can join via the Veteran Employment Commitment. Resources such as the Veteran Employment Toolkit, the Core Skills Identifier and an interactive list of veteran employers are available for veterans and their families.[[96]]

items.title: Department of Veterans’ Affairs, Veteran Support and Services Guide 2025
summaryParagraphs: Highlights the support and services available for veterans. Provides a link to programs and support services offered by Federal and State/Territory Government departments.[[97]]

items.title: Government of Western Australia, Department of Premier and Cabinet – Veteran Employment
summaryParagraphs: Provides information on available opportunities and initiatives for veterans seeking employment in the civilian workforce. Last updated in 2024, the Veteran Employment service outlines Veteran Employment Opportunities through organisations such as Jobs & Skills WA, the Defence Industry Veterans Employment Scheme (DIVES) Scholarship Program for VET and university studies available to eligible veterans (as well as information for potential employers).[[98]]

items.title: Government of Western Australia, Defence Industry – The Other Force Veterans Defence Industry Career Explorer
summaryParagraphs: Assists veterans in understanding how their skills and experience align to occupations in Western Australia’s defence industry and identifies possible career pathways.[[99]]

items.title: New South Wales Government Rank to Grade Guide and Local Government Rank to Grade Guide
summaryParagraphs: Provides veterans with guidance and understanding on how NSW Government and Local Government job grades align to ADF ranks. Tool for employers to understand the skills and experience that veterans can bring to their organisation.[[100]]

items.title: New South Wales Veterans Employment Program (VEP)
summaryParagraphs: Provides veterans with tools to assist in applying for roles in the NSW public service, as well as to employers. The VEP has published online resources, such as a capability definition tool and access to workshops to support veterans in their application to NSW public sector positions.[[101]]

items.title: New South Wales Veterans Strategy and Action Plan, 2025-2030
summaryParagraphs: Outlines key themes and the actions that the NSW Government is taking to support its veterans. It is intended to be a ‘first step’ in response to the Royal Commission into Defence and Veterans Suicide and as part of its scope, provides information on the translation of Defence-specific capabilities into civilian requirements.[[102]]

items.title: Northern Territory Government, Defence Veterans Strategy
summaryParagraphs: Provides outcomes, case studies and lists supports and actions for veterans and their families in the Northern Territory, to assist in the transition out of Defence and ensure access to employment opportunities.[[103]]

items.title: TAFE NSW Ranks to Recognition
summaryParagraphs: Supports ADF personnel and veterans in their transition to the civilian workforce by assessing and recognising skills, experience and qualifications gained during military service with the intended outcome of a smooth transition for ADF personnel in accessing career opportunities and/or further study. Delivered in partnership with the NSW Office of Veterans Affairs.[[104]]

items.title: TAFE SA Skills Transition Education Program (STEP)
summaryParagraphs: Provides serving and ex-serving ADF personnel and their families with support to transition to the civilian workforce via career planning, funding assistance to access VET and Recognition of Prior Learning.[[105]]

items.title: Veterans Queensland
summaryParagraphs: Coordinates contact with multiple functions, including supporting employment pathways for ex-ADF personnel into the Queensland Government and key industries like logistic (as well as information for employers).[[106]]

items.title: Veterans South Australia
summaryParagraphs: Provides information on available services, programs and opportunities in South Australia for Defence veterans and their families. To support veteran transition to the civilian workforce, programs such as the South Australian Veteran Employer Network were established. Veterans South Australia also promotes and supports programs run by other organisations, such as TAFE SA’s STEP.[[107]]

items.title: Victorian Government Veterans Employment Workshops
summaryParagraphs: Supports veterans in exploring potential career pathways through workshops held regularly by the Office for Veterans. Workshops provide an opportunity for veterans to connect and network with HR representatives, employers, personnel and other veterans.[[108]]

items.title: Victorian Public Sector, Employing Veterans in the Victorian Public Sector
summaryParagraphs: Provides a central hub for veterans to register for employment opportunities in the Victorian Public Sector (VPS). Provides general guidance on rank across the ADF and their approximate equivalent in the VPS. Provides mentor opportunities, information about networking events and case studies. The initiatives outlined by the Victorian Government put into practice the Public Sector Veteran Employment Strategy (2016).[[109]]

summaryParagraphs: Demand for services: Demand for both firefighter and state and territory emergency services (SES) increased by 7.6 per cent from 488,242 (total combined emergency response activities) in 2019–20 to 525,346 in 2023–24.[[43]] 40 major emergency incidents were documented from July 2024 to June 2025 (an increase from 30 the previous year).[[44]]

items.title: Career and Volunteer firefighters and emergency services employees
summaryParagraphs: Career and Volunteer firefighters and emergency services employees: In the 20 years from August 2005 to August 2025, the career Fire and Emergency Services occupation (ANZSCO 4412) experienced a 65.9 per cent growth, outpacing the wider job market at 48.4 per cent.[[45]] This is supported by growth in student enrolments from 2019 to 2024 in the two core qualifications required for firefighters. Similarly, the total career operational and support emergency services personnel have experienced year-on-year increases since 2019–20.[[46]]

Volunteer services: Compared to career firefighting, total volunteer firefighter numbers (including support staff) decreased by nearly 12,000 volunteers from 2019–20 to 2024–25.[[48]] Similarly, SES has largely experienced year-on-year declines in total volunteers since 2019–20, in line with wider decline in volunteerism trends.[[49]]

Despite relative increases in career Firefighter and operational SES members from 2019–20 to 2024–25, in absolute terms, the increases in career employees are heavily negated by the decreases experienced in volunteer cohorts. Collectively, in the five years from 2019–2025, a total of 1,130 career Firefighters and SES members were added to Australia’s emergency response capability, while a total of 10,336 volunteers were lost.

items.title: Surf Life Saving
summaryParagraphs: Surf Life Saving: Across 2024–2025, Surf Life Saving provided a combined total of 1.95 million hours of lifesaving patrol activity, with New South Wales and Queensland accounting for more than 70 per cent of total hours served.[[50]] This enabled a combined total of 2.19 million preventative actions, along with 65,942 administrations of first aid and 8,207 rescues across both volunteer and career surf lifesavers.[[51]]

blocks.title: Major emergency incidents and the Royal Commission in 2020
paragraphs: From July 2024 to June 2025, the Australian Institute for Disaster Resilience Major Incidents Report documented 40 major emergency incidents, spanning fires, floods, storms, tropical cyclones, health outbreaks, technology failures and repatriations from international conflict zones.[[53]] This is an increase from both the 2022–23 and 2023–24 financial years as detailed to the right:

Fire and Emergency Services stakeholders noted that at the time of the Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements in 2020 (Royal Commission in 2020), specialist disaster recovery skills and functions were identified as different to those required in emergency management. Following the Royal Commission in 2020, a suite of nationally accredited training products related to disaster recovery were developed.[[55]] Facilitated through the National Recovery Training Program,[[56]] newly developed disaster recovery training products included one qualification, nine skill sets and four units of competency (refer Appendix B – Disaster recovery training products from the Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements).

Collectively, these training products are targeted at individuals without emergency service backgrounds, including local community members, social service providers, local government personnel, spontaneous volunteers or individuals from government organisations tasked with recovery coordination.[[57]]

paragraphs: Public Safety Workforce Insights Report
Theme One, Insight Three

Australia is experiencing a critical challenge in maintaining capability to use fire effectively in the landscape, particularly for complex prescribed burning and backburning during bushfire suppression.

blocks.title: Community recovery and prescribed burning
paragraphs: As described in the National Principles for Disaster Recovery, community involvement in disaster recovery activities is critical for ensuring long-term disaster recovery success and community resilience.[[60]] Consequently, access to relevant and contemporary disaster recovery training is required to enable community, local government, and state, territory and federal government personnel and volunteers to adequately support communities in times of disaster.

Connected to this is the role of prescribed burning in decreasing the scale of recovery efforts required after a major fire. Prescribed burning reduces fuel hazards and can assist the success of suppression activities and reduce the intensity, extent and impacts of subsequent bushfires. At the same time, insights gained during disaster recovery, such as patterns of fire behaviour, infrastructure vulnerability and ecological impacts can directly inform the planning and prioritisation of prescribed burns.[[61]]

However, capability in the use of prescribed burning is declining. Changes in rural land use, primary industries and forest management, together with shifting policies for fire, land management, emergency services and the environment at different levels of government have contributed to the challenges of maintaining skills.

The Australasian Fire and Emergency Services Authorities Council (AFAC) in conjunction with the Forest Fire Management Group developed a series of documents including principles, frameworks and guidelines as part of the National Burning Project. These documents are aimed at developing nationally consistent approaches to the use of prescribed burning by the Fire and Emergency Services industry-sector. This prescribed burning capability is supported by five units of competency in the PUA Public Safety Training Package.[[62]]

paragraphs: Public Safety Workforce Insights Report
Theme Two, Insight One
The HLTAID010 unit of competency is an entry-level first aid training product that is no longer meeting the operational needs for volunteer surf lifesavers.

blocks.title: HLTAID010 and HLTAID011 compared
paragraphs: In 2024–25, volunteer surf lifesavers administered six times more first aid treatments compared to rescue operations. The number of yearly first aid treatments administered has also been increasing year-on-year since 2022–23.[[63]] This highlights a distinct operational capability requirement for volunteers. Skilling of volunteer surf lifesavers is provided through the PUA20119 Certificate II in Public Safety (Aquatic Rescue).

The importance of this qualification is strongly supported by its high utilisation with more than 1,500 completions per year since 2020.[[64]] The principal first aid unit of competency in this qualification is HLTAID010 Provide Basic Emergency Life Support. Recent consultation with industry stakeholders identified that this unit of competency is not meeting the increasing first aid requirements of Surf Life Saving.

Stakeholders identified that the HLTAID011 Provide First Aid unit of competency is considered a more complete resource for providing the increasing first aid skills demands for volunteer surf lifesavers. The differences between the training products are the range of medical conditions and injuries trained to be treated.
