paragraphs: Public Safety Workforce Insights Report
Theme Three, Insight One

Incidents involving hazardous materials are becoming increasingly important while current training may be limiting in some Fire and Emergency Services organisations ability to deliver this type of service.

blocks.title: Hazardous materials incidents and training
paragraphs: Each year, firefighting organisations around Australia respond to a range of emergency incidents. In 2024–25, this included, but was not limited to, 11,982 incidents relating to hazardous materials.[[65]] Specific to responding to hazardous materials incidents, training is enabled through three units of competency in the PUA Public Safety Training Package:
Identify, detect and monitor hazardous materials at an incident
Employ personal protection at a hazardous materials incident
Render hazardous materials incidents safe
The importance of these three units of competency is supported by annual enrolment data, with all three products having high use rates since 2020.

Chart source: National Centre for Vocational Education Research (NCVER), Total VET students and courses 2024: DataBuilder, [subject enrolments, subject data set], NCVER, 2025, accessed 17 December 2025.

Due to evolving technology and access to different equipment across organisations, stakeholders indicated that some aspects of PUAFIR306 Identify, detect and monitor hazardous materials at an incident may require updating. Specifically, this unit of competency may require an update related to the use of gas detection equipment and certain personal protective equipment (PPE) and personal protective clothing (PPC), which, as a prerequisite unit, may limit access to other training units.

In its current form, this unit of competency excludes some firefighting organisations that either use different equipment or do not have access to specific equipment detailed in the unit of competency.

Additionally, PUAFIR306 is a pre-requisite unit of competency in PUASAR025 Undertake confined space rescue – a highly utilised unit of competency across both the Mining and Public Safety industries.[[66]] This unit of competency is also utilised across all states and territories, with 8,871 subject enrolments in 2024 alone.

Some industry-sector representatives expressed challenges with some of the prescriptive requirements in the units of competency that may impact some agencies being able to deliver and award these qualifications. Further to this, some terminology and assessment conditions were identified as potential limiting factors in training employees in these units of competency.

While response to incidents involving hazardous materials is becoming increasingly important, the specificity of equipment requirements in current training may be limiting access by Fire and Emergency Services organisations to other training units, impacting national response capabilities.

Recent consultation with stakeholders highlighted the importance of the link between the two units of competency and advise that any updates to this hazardous materials unit of competency must carefully consider any potential downstream impacts on other training products.

Further consensus must be built to ensure any proposed training solutions meet the needs of all industry representatives, including ensuring that employee organisations are supportive of any proposed alternatives.

items.title: Support uptake of disaster recovery training products (Refer Appendix B for list of training products)
items.objective: Strengthen capabilities of disaster recovery for Fire and Emergency Services and Government personnel by promoting the uptake of disaster recovery training products.
approach: Develop and implement a promotion plan for disaster recovery products among TAFEs and RTOs.
deliverable: Presentation of promotions to RTO, TAFE and stakeholders

items.title: Review first aid units of competency for Surf Life Saving in the Certificate II in Public Safety (Aquatic Rescue)

approach: This strategy will collaborate with Surf Life Saving Australia and state/territory Surf Life Saving organisations to compare the level of current first aid training units of competency with current skill requirements in surf lifesaving. items.impact: Equip surf lifesavers with the skills required to meet current and future needs in keeping Australia’s coastline safe.

items.title: Review prerequisite requirements for PUAFIR306 Identify, detect and monitor hazardous materials at an incident
items.objective: Support increased access to hazardous materials training by reviewing a key unit of competency for the Fire and Emergency Services industry.
approach: This strategy will engage with key Fire and Emergency Services employers and unions, and mining stakeholders (through AUSMASA) to review the PUAFIR306 Identify, detect and monitor hazardous materials at an incident and PUASAR025 Undertake confined space rescue units of competency.
items.impact: Increase accessible training to enable safe and effective hazardous materials response.

summaryParagraphs: To identify drivers and challenges to recruiting, engaging and retaining youth volunteers.

detailSections.heading: Update
paragraphs: In collaboration with Fire and Emergency Services volunteer organisations, this project aims to strengthen youth volunteer retention in Fire and Emergency Services by identifying the key drivers of attraction, recruitment and sustained engagement.

A literature review was undertaken to inform the research design. This was followed by a facilitated workshop with a wide range of Fire and Emergency Services youth volunteer stakeholders. Initial feedback has indicated that while young people are highly motivated by a desire to contribute to their community, they often face barriers such as competing study and work commitments, and limited structural development pathways.
When complete, this project will produce an evidence-based Insights Report outlining findings for organisations relating to attracting, recruiting, engaging and retaining youth volunteers.

items.title: National Disaster Risk Reduction Framework
summaryParagraphs: The National Disaster Risk Reduction Framework was developed as an advancement to the 2011 National Strategy for Disaster Resilience and in line with the global Sendai Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030. The framework was co-designed by all levels of government, industry and community representatives and intends to guide Australia's capability in reducing “disaster risk associated with natural hazards”.
The four priorities of the framework are:

In August 2023, the Second National Action Plan was endorsed by all Emergency Management Ministers and provides an update on how the National Disaster Risk Reduction Framework can continue to be implemented. Specifically, National Action 21 describes that Australia must “Better align recovery and resilience activities, governance, funding, policy and processes to support betterment and long-term disaster risk reduction.”

items.title: Australian Disaster Recovery Framework
summaryParagraphs: This framework provides a practical and comprehensive description of disaster recovery context, governance, doctrine and policy. Although each state and territory in Australia has their own disaster recovery policies, the framework provides a common understanding for how disaster recovery can be undertaken.

The framework further supports recovery activities for all individuals that may be involved in recovery, including practitioners or leaders at all levels of government, private companies, community personnel and charities. As the stewards of the framework, NEMA will review the framework periodically as required.

paragraphs: Public Safety Workforce Insights Report
Theme One, Insight One
Skills shortages and strong demand for similar skills may require the establishment of multiple entry pathways for digital forensic professionals into policing.

blocks.title: Demand for digital forensics
paragraphs: Broader digital transformation and the increasing adoption of technology means that evidence can be found on a growing array of devices, such as computer systems, mobile phones, cars, doorbells and dog collars.[[69]] According to testimonial evidence in the United Kingdom, most criminal investigations now contain elements of digital evidence that require retrieval and examination by digital forensic experts, whether from computers, mobile phones, CCTV, GPS systems or other digital devices.[[70]]

Despite the increased demand for digital forensics, there has not been a corresponding uplift in capability and coordination in this area.[[71]] This has led to a substantial backlog of digital forensics work.[[72]] Stakeholder consultations in Australia indicated that digital forensics required to support contemporary investigations needs a different set of skills to other forensic field sciences such as fingerprint and firearms examination. Digital evidence is more easily destroyed, can span multiple jurisdictions and is evolving at a rapid pace.[[73]]

blocks.title: Three domains of digital forensic skills
paragraphs: Through consultations, it was identified that digital forensic skills required in policing covers three domains:
bullets: Foundation skills across policing: Police working on investigations involving digital evidence require an understanding of how data has been gathered, acquired and any limitations that data may have, in the same way as they would need to understand physical forensic evidence.[[74]] It is critical that police involved in digital evidence collection know how to collect and store data without altering it, given that seemingly harmless actions such as opening, printing or saving files can change metadata permanently and place the evidence in question.[[75]]

Core Digital Forensic Examiner Skills: Digital forensic examiners must have a core set of skills and must be adaptable and focus on problem solving as they work with ever changing digital environments. They must be able to continually adapt to changes in technology, operating system and devices.[[76]]

Specialist Digital Forensics Roles: In addition to the foundational and core digital examiner skills, consultation identified that there are likely several specialist digital forensic areas requiring more advanced skills. This would include an Advanced Digital Forensic Examiner, Mobile Device Forensic Specialist, Cloud and Network Forensics Specialist and Quality Assurance / Technical Reviewer.

blocks.title: Skills shortages and entry pathways
paragraphs: Cyber Security Professionals, including digital forensic specialists, is a segment of the workforce that is experiencing sustained demand, with employment in this group projected to grow 14.2 per cent between 2024 and 2029.[[77]] This is more than double the national average rate of growth at 6.6 per cent.[[78]]

As there is significant cross-over in the digital skills required by the private sector and those in demand for digital forensics in policing, this gives rise to competition with the private sector where wages are generally higher.

Persistent shortages of skilled cyber employees have been noted, with Jobs and Skills Australia’s Occupation Shortage List analysis finding several cyber security occupations in national shortage, indicating challenges in filling vacancies for most jurisdictions.[[79]] This is likely compounded by the wider recruitment and retention challenge policing has faced in recent years. Skills shortages and strong demand for similar skills may require the establishment of multiple entry pathways for digital forensic professionals.

blocks.title: The POL Police Training Package
paragraphs: Theme One, Insight Two

The VET system is well established to deliver a nationally consistent approach to training, however, the Police Training Package currently does not contain a qualification specialising in digital forensics.

Internationally, alternative pathways have been established including paid internships for ex-defence personnel that include digital forensics training and apprenticeship schemes that offer a pathway into a career in digital forensics.[[80]] Additionally, establishing career pathways needs be considered as a part of overall workforce planning approaches particularly to retain younger cohorts in the digital forensics roles.[[81]]

Stakeholder consultation identified that the POL Police Training Package could be leveraged to develop much needed digital forensics skills. Internationally, a lack of consistency in digital forensics training has been identified as a risk to both the efficiency and quality of digital forensic investigations. Developing training products through the VET system will provide police nationally consistent, industry-endorsed skills standards that will support mitigating the risks encountered internationally.

Additionally, these skills could be developed to cover general duties police officers right through to digital forensic specialist roles, ensuring police can develop consistent skills for handling digital forensics evidence.[[82]]

pages.title: 2. Rural, Regional and Remote Police Leadership

content.badge: Theme 2. Rural, Regional and Remote Police Leadership. Insight One
content.headerTitle: 2. Rural, Regional and Remote Police Leadership

paragraphs: Public Safety Workforce Insights Report
Theme Two, Insight One

Police officers are being required to take on more leadership responsibilities earlier in their careers – particularly in regional, rural and remote areas, which may require more support in accelerating leadership skills development.

blocks.title: Workforce shortages in regional, rural and remote communities
paragraphs: As a whole, police have experienced workforce shortages driven by two years of FTE reductions in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. Unlike the large patrols and area commands in metropolitan areas, regional, rural and remote communities police stations often deploy fewer than five officers, with some stations deploying only one or two officers.[[83]] As such, the ripple effects of workforce shortages have a greater impact on regional, rural and remote communities where the loss of only one or two police officers equates to a large proportion of the operational capacity in these communities.[[84]]

Alongside workforce shortages, recruitment challenges for regional, rural and remote communities can make it difficult for police jurisdictions to increase the number of officers deployed in these communities.[[85]] While most police jurisdictions have established incentive programs to encourage regional, rural and remote placements,[[86]] engagement with industry-sector stakeholders indicated that shortages in regional, rural and remote locations are persisting.

blocks.title: Earlier leadership responsibilities
paragraphs: Industry-sector consultation identified that these shortages, alongside wider demographic shifts and higher turnover in policing in recent years, has resulted in police officers being required to take on more leadership responsibilities earlier in their careers. This means that those police officers may not have the depth of experience to draw from when having to take on these leadership roles and may require greater levels of support to accelerate the development of their leadership skills.

Further industry consultation confirmed that, while this is an area that required more examination, there is no direct requirement for any training product development or implementation, promotion and monitoring activity.

items.title: Organisation Capability Review
summaryParagraphs: The WA Police Force Organisation Capability Review (2023-24) calls for a clear long-term strategy to enhance operational effectiveness, workforce planning and inter-organisation collaboration.

The final report was delivered in November 2024. This report provides observations across 21 capabilities, identified three lines of inquiry for in depth investigation and highlighted two areas of strength.

As part of the review, comment was provided on the future operating environment for the WA Police Force. This included identifying that officers will need to become increasingly proficient in the areas of cybercrime, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.
WA Police Force is yet to publicly respond to the review.

leadParagraphs: The 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report proposes six strategies across the Defence, Fire and Emergency Services and Police industry-sectors. These strategies aim to build on and/or complement the existing strategies that were proposed through the 2025 Public Safety Workforce Insights report and have been completed or continue to be progressed.

items.title: Support Defence skill and capability requirements to operationalise drones
items.intro: Map current Defence micro-credentials on drones and unmanned aerial systems (UAS) to existing units of competency from current VET qualifications.
items.objective: Map current Defence micro-credentials on drones and unmanned aerial systems (UAS) to existing units of competency from current VET qualifications.
approach: Identify whether current units of competency relating to UAS and drones meet the skills requirements of Defence. Should gaps be found, review or develop new units of competency to address these gaps.
items.impact: Support the Defence workforce by enabling rapid, targeted upskilling in UAS and drone-related technologies.
stakeholders: Defence Education, Learning and Training Authority (DELTA)

items.title: Support uptake of disaster recovery training products
items.intro: Strengthen capabilities of disaster recovery for Fire and Emergency Services and Government personnel by promoting the uptake of disaster recovery training products.
items.objective: Strengthen capabilities of disaster recovery for Fire and Emergency Services and Government personnel by promoting the uptake of disaster recovery training products.
approach: Develop and implement a promotion plan for disaster recovery products among TAFEs and RTOs.
deliverable: Presentation of promotions to RTO, TAFE and stakeholders
items.impact: Capability uplift across Fire and Emergency Services and Government personnel through increased uptake of nationally consistent disaster recovery training.

items.title: Develop Training Products for Digital Forensics
items.intro: Develop a digital forensics qualification to be included in the POL Police Training Package.
items.objective: Develop a digital forensics qualification to be included in the POL Police Training Package.
approach: Engage the Australia New Zealand Policing Advisory Agency (ANZPAA) and the National Institute of Forensic Science to develop a digital forensics qualification, supported by specialist advisory groups.
items.impact: Develop a nationally consistent approach to training digital forensics for policing and support addressing an area of skills shortage.
stakeholders: State/Territory Police organisations and Australian Federal Police

items.title: Support transition of Defence Veterans to civilian workforce
items.intro: Support Recommendation 83(c) of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide by facilitating up-to-date information facilitated by state and territory initiatives that assist transitioning veterans.
items.objective: Support Recommendation 83(c) of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide by supporting up-to-date information facilitated by state and territory initiatives that assist transitioning veterans.
approach: Collaborate with Defence to map ADF job roles and training to the Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) levels and approximate equivalent civilian qualifications.Develop material that translates military terminology into civilian contexts, to build collective understanding for both transitioning veterans and prospective civilian employers.Collaborate with Defence to share this information back through state and territories to be included on their websites for veterans.
items.impact: Support Recommendation 83(c) by providing information through Defence, states and territories that support veterans to translate their Defence skills and experience into civilian-recognised language.
stakeholders: Defence Education, Learning and Training Authority (DELTA)

items.title: Review first aid units of competency for Surf Life Saving in the Certificate II in Public Safety (Aquatic Rescue)
items.intro: Ensure the Certificate II in Public Safety (Aquatic Rescue) reflects the first aid requirements of Surf Life Saving.
items.objective: Ensure the Certificate II in Public Safety (Aquatic Rescue) reflects the first aid requirements of Surf Life Saving.
approach: Collaborate with Surf Life Saving Australia and state/territory organisations to compare the level of current first aid training units with the skills required in surf lifesaving. This may result in an update to the Certificate II in Public Safety (Aquatic Rescue).
items.impact: Equip surf lifesavers with the skills required to meet current and future needs in keeping Australia’s coastline safe.

items.title: Review prerequisite requirements for PUAFIR306 Identify, detect and monitor hazardous materials at an incident
items.intro: Support increased access to hazardous materials training though reviewing a key unit of competency for the Fire and Emergency Services industry.
items.objective: Support increased access to hazardous materials training by reviewing a key unit of competency for the Fire and Emergency Services industry.
approach: Engage with key Fire and Emergency Services employers and unions, and mining stakeholders through AUSMASA, to review the PUAFIR306 Identify, detect and monitor hazardous materials at an incident and PUASAR025 Undertake confined space rescue units of competency.
items.impact: Increase accessible training to enable safe and effective hazardous materials response.

leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia's work is informed and guided by the Commonwealth Government initiatives detailed below.

items.eyebrow: National Cabinet (formerly Council of Australian Governments)
items.title: National Agreement on Closing the Gap (Closing the Gap)
summaryParagraphs: Closing the Gap is a commitment from all Australian governments and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander representatives to a fundamentally new way of developing and implementing policies and programs that impact the lives of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. This includes policies and programs impacting recruitment, health and social programs specific to First Nations peoples, which are relevant to the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors.

Closing the Gap is jointly implemented by the Federal, State and Territory governments, along with the Australian Local Government Association and the Coalition of Peaks. It focuses on four priority reforms: strengthening formal partnerships and shared decision-making; building the community-controlled sector; transforming government organisations; and shared access to data. It also includes 19 national socio-economic targets covering areas such as life expectancy, education, employment, justice and child protection. Overall progress towards meeting Closing the Gap targets has been mixed. Implementation is ongoing to 2031 and the Productivity Commission is tracking these targets.

Closing the Gap reaffirms a substantive role in informing Public Skills Australia's research and engagement efforts. It informed stakeholder consultation preparation as part of engagement for the 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report.

items.eyebrow: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
items.title: The Australian Government’s Strategic Priorities
summaryParagraphs: The Federal Government's strategic priorities provide a four-year (2022–2026) policy direction for the Australian Public Service (APS) and set targets across key areas. These areas include the economy, public health and climate change.

The Australian Government's Strategic Priorities are split into the first year of their implementation by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet with the relevant APS departments and organisations. So far, the Strategic Priorities, which have not been placed on set timelines, have achieved several outcomes, including hosting a Jobs and Skills Summit; developing a plan for cheaper child care; implementing fee-free TAFE and creating more university places; establishing the National Reconstruction Fund; introducing legislation for a national anti-corruption commission; and strengthening strategic partnerships in the Pacific and South East Asia. Progress is still required for public health and aged care, improving housing supply and planning reforms, and advancing government budget sustainability.

The "strong, inclusive and sustainable economy" priority supported the development of the Support transition of Defence Veterans to civilian workforce proposed project, which looks to ensure veterans can translate their Defence skills and experience into civilian-recognised language and occupations, inclusive of those in the APS where relevant.

items.title: Working for Women – A Strategy for Gender Equality
summaryParagraphs: The Working for Women Strategy outlines a framework for the Australian Government to improve national gender equality. It sets out five priority areas and reports on a range of outcomes and indicators annually to monitor Australia's progress. These priority areas are:
Specific to JSCs, Priority Area 3 focuses on improving gender pay gaps, supporting access to skills and training and reducing occupational and industrial gender segregation.

To date, the Australian Government has increased female recruitment into trades and other occupations through apprenticeship support, fee-free TAFE and targets in the Australian Skills Guarantee, along with including gender equality as a national priority in the National Skills Agreement.

In March 2025, the Department for Workplace Relations launched the Advancing Gender Equality in Gender Segregated Industries grant program, directly linked to Priority Area 3. This grant program received a $28.5 million extension in December 2025.

Priority Area 3 of the Working for Women strategy informed Public Skills Australia's approach to the 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report by ensuring that stakeholder consultations considered any workforce challenges that may be linked to women's economic equality or participation in Public Safety occupations. Future directions identified in Priority Area 3 highlight the need for "action to embed gender equality to support access and retention for women in emerging and growth industries, like clean energy, cyber security and naval ship and submarine building." Public Skills Australia will continue to work closely with industry to progress gender equality in these emerging areas.
bullets: Priority Area 2 – Unpaid and paid care
Priority Area 3 – Economic equality and security
Priority Area 5 – Leadership, representation and decision making

items.title: The Clean Energy Generation: Workforce needs for a Net Zero Economy
summaryParagraphs: This series of reports considers emerging and future clean-energy workforce requirements as Australia strives to reach net-zero emissions by 2050. JSA's preliminary modelling estimates Australia's clean-energy workforce will need to grow from the current 53,000 employees to 84,000 employees by 2050.

The report makes 50 recommendations to support governments in focusing their efforts on how skills shortages can be averted in the set time, resources and legislative constraints and government objectives. Broadly, the recommendations cover the challenge areas of participation and attraction, hiring and retention, transitioning employees and communities, roles and responsibilities, critical occupations, education and training and transport. Implementation remains ongoing and long-term, aligned with the 2050 net-zero target.

This series of reports, specifically, the recommendations made within the reports, informed preparation for stakeholder consultation as part of research and engagement for the 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report. These recommendations provided context on where future skilling and occupational priorities may exist and how technology may change that impacts how Public Safety occupations are experienced.

items.title: Australian Cyber Security Strategy
summaryParagraphs: The 2023–2030 Australian Cyber Security Strategy serves as a roadmap to achieve the Australian Government's vision of becoming a world leader in cyber security by 2030.

The Strategy is structured around six 'cyber shields' (strong citizens and businesses, safe technology, world-class threat sharing, protected critical infrastructure, sovereign capability and resilient regional/global leadership). These are to be delivered in three stages or 'Horizons' (2023–2025 strengthening the foundations, 2026–2028 scaling efforts across the whole economy and 2029–2030 leading the development of new cyber technologies). Progress to date has focused on the foundational aspects of the Strategy, with the initial work under 'Horizon 1' (2023–2025) concentrating on improving incident reporting and response mechanisms, introducing legislative reforms, piloting threat-sharing initiatives and raising government and critical infrastructure security standards. Overall coordination sits with the Department of Home Affairs, specifically through the Australian Cyber Security Coordinator. The remaining two horizons are to be implemented over the next four years up to 2030.

This ongoing cyber security work provided important contextual background for stakeholder consultation preparation for the 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report and informed the development of the Develop Training Products for Digital Forensics project. Specifically, cyber security and skills related to cyber security are similar to those required in digital forensics and may provide a useful reference point for developing digital forensics training.

items.title: Unlocking the Potential of VET
summaryParagraphs: In March 2024, the Qualification Reform Design Group (QRDG) provided advice to Skills Ministers on reforming the Vocational Education and Training (VET) qualifications system. This included advising that:

As a result, Public Skills Australia undertook a Demonstration Project that consulted widely to determine the efficacy of updating qualification and unit of competency templates. This report was delivered to the QRDG in Q3 2024.

In December 2024, the QRDG provided their final report and recommendations to Skills Minsters, based on national consultation and findings from the JSC Demonstration Projects. The recommendations from this report centred around modernising VET qualifications by implementing a purpose-led, principles-based approach to qualification design. As a result, JSCs are responsible for ensuring qualifications serve a clear purpose, are linked to workforce needs and are not unnecessarily duplicated.

The work of the QRDG regarding qualification reform continues to inform the method and intended outcomes for all proposed strategies that may result in training package updates, including Support Defence skill and capability requirements to operationalise drones, Review first aid Units of Competency for Surf Life Saving in the Certificate II in Public Safety (Aquatic Rescue), Review prerequisite requirements for PUAFIR306 Identify, detect and monitor hazardous materials at an incident and PUASAR025 Undertake confined space rescue, and Develop Training Products for Digital Forensics.
bullets: Qualification and unit of competency design and development processes should be reviewed and updated where appropriate.
The VET system should be consolidated by removing training products that are underutilised or unnecessarily duplicated.
The Training Package Organising Framework should be updated, where necessary.

items.title: Occupation Standard Classification for Australia
summaryParagraphs: Formally known as Australia New Zealand Standard Classification of Occupation (ANZSCO), the Occupation Standard Classification for Australia (OSCA) is a standardised framework for classifying occupations in Australia. As part of the replacement process from ANZSCO to OSCA in 2024, the ABS announced that OSCA will undergo regular updates in accordance with the OSCA Maintenance Strategy, which was released in 2025.

Changes to OSCA outlined in the Maintenance Strategy, involve stakeholder engagement and are timed to ensure that each Census of Population and Housing uses the most recent update. Under the strategy, the first round of consultations and feedback with stakeholders on proposed changes to OSCA are scheduled to be completed in August 2026, with the next update to be published in March 2027 before the data release of the 2026 Census in October 2027.
Public Skills Australia continues to utilise, where possible, the most contemporary version of OSCA to ensure our occupational insights remain relevant and in-line with whole-of-economy standards.

items.title: 2024 Core Skills Occupation List – Key Findings Report
summaryParagraphs: The Core Skills Occupation List (CSOL) provides labour market analysis that informs the identification of occupations that are considered appropriate for employer-sponsored temporary migration through the Core Skills Stream of the Skills in Demand (SID) Visa.

The 2024 CSOL Key Findings Report compiled a list of 456 occupations considered appropriate for the Core Skills Stream of the new employer-sponsored temporary SID visa. In addition to updating the list, JSA examined the drivers of skill shortages through CSOL analysis and stakeholder engagement and identified a 'suitability gap' category – occupations where there are enough qualified applicants, but they are not regarded as suitable by employers (e.g. auditors, electronics engineers, software and applications programmers). JSA also identified a 'retention gap' category – occupations with below-average rates of retention such as construction and hospitality jobs and child carers. JSA's consultations to inform the 2025 CSOL opened in August 2025 and JSA submitted its advice to Government for consideration in October 2025.

Along with the Jobs and Skills Australia Occupational Shortage List, the CSOL (specifically the 2025 CSOL Targeted for Consultation Group) provided important context for stakeholder consultation preparation for the 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report. These lists indicate on a national level where specific occupation demands may currently exist and enabled Public Skills Australia to proactively pursue conversations with Public Safety stakeholders on whether these demands exist within their contexts.

items.title: Better Together – The Jobs and Skills Report 2024
summaryParagraphs: This report was released in November 2024 as part of JSA's mandated obligations to provide insight on the Australian labour market and advice on workforce needs and priorities. This report details evidence aligned to five strategic pillars to enable a more prosperous economic future, including:

Better Together outlines JSA's key current and emerging datasets that provide useful insights on the intricacies of Australia's labour market for use in development of strategic workforce planning for the JSCs. Please note JSA released an updated version of this iterative report in November 2025, Connecting for Impact – The Jobs and Skills Report 2025, which will inform the 2027 Workforce Insights Reports.

The outcomes of Better Together provided important context on whole-of-economy skilling and training needs. For the 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report, these outcomes informed the development of the Support Defence skill and capability requirements to operationalise drones strategy that aims to ensure the Defence industry-sector maintains a future-ready workforce.
bullets: Fostering inclusive participation: Focused on broadening employment opportunities through identifying and removing barriers for people and communities.
Understanding today's workforce: Detailing data to build an evidence base that informs and addresses current and emerging labour market and skills needs.
Shaping Australia's future workforce: Projecting forward to plan for the opportunities and challenges of Australia's future workforce needs.
Optimising pathways and system architecture: Monitoring, analysing and advising on the effectiveness of the Vocational Education and Training (VET) system as key to skilling the workforce.

Activating an informed dialogue: Detailing stakeholder engagement across the VET system to provide the best evidence and advice on Australia's current and future workforce and skills needs and opportunities.

items.title: Training Package Organising Framework
summaryParagraphs: In July 2025, the Training Package Organising Framework (TPOF) was updated based on advice from the QRDG in December 2024. Housing the Training Package Products Development and Endorsement Process Policy (TPPDEPP), Training Package Products Policy (TPPP) and the Standards for Training Packages, the TPOF sets out the process for developing and seeking approval of new VET training products for JSCs. As a JSC, Public Skills Australia will continue to adhere to the TPOF to ensure the Australian VET system is high-performing and readily supports student and industry needs.

The updated TPOF provides specific guidance to all projects that may result in changes to any training products. This includes the 2026 proposed workforce strategies Support Defence skill and capability requirements to operationalise drones, Review first aid Units of Competency for Surf Life Saving in the Certificate II in Public Safety (Aquatic Rescue), Review prerequisite requirements for PUAFIR306 Identify, detect and monitor hazardous materials at an incident and PUASAR025 Undertake confined space rescue, and Develop Training Products for Digital Forensics.

items.title: Five pillars of productivity inquiries – final reports
summaryParagraphs: The Productivity Commission has provided 47 recommendations across 'five pillars' of productivity policy:
At the time of drafting this report, the Australian Government is yet to provide response to the recommendations.

The recommendations of these reports, especially those in the 'Building a skilled and adaptable workforce' report, informed the development of all seven proposed strategies in the 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report. Recommendations such as Recommendation 3.1 Improve the recognition of work-related training provide important guidance when considering how the VET system can support and enhance whole-of-economy productivity.
bullets: Creating a more dynamic and resilient economy.
Building a skilled and adaptable workforce.
Investing in cheaper, cleaner energy and the net zero transformation.

items.title: Opportunity and Productivity: Towards a Tertiary Harmonisation Roadmap Report
summaryParagraphs: This report seeks to articulate the benefits of a more harmonised tertiary sector and provides recommendations on how to create a sustainable pathway forward in collaboration with key stakeholders. It outlines 19 key recommendations, across three categories (Enabling the tertiary harmonisation roadmap; Early priorities for the roadmap and medium-term horizon roadmap priorities), to work towards a harmonised system that can tackle national challenges, address skilled workforce shortages and improve productivity.

This Report provided important context in preparation for stakeholder consultation for the 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report through its emphasis on productivity, improved student experience and enhancing inflows of appropriately skilled individuals into the workforce.

items.title: Gender Economic Equality Study
summaryParagraphs: The Gender Economic Equality Study explored three challenges for the jobs and skills systems that contribute to gender economic inequality:

The study was reported over three papers, with the third and final paper Speeding up progress towards gender economic equality being released in October 2025. This paper sets out 10 recommendations to address challenges in the jobs and skills system that perpetuate inequality and impact productivity:

This study informed Public Skills Australia's approach to the 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report by ensuring that stakeholder consultations considered any workforce challenges that may be linked to women's economic equality or participation in Public Safety occupations. Public Skills Australia will utilise the GSIS in future work, where relevant, to provide important insight on gender trends in Public Safety occupations.

items.title: Occupational Shortage List
summaryParagraphs: The Occupational Shortage List (OSL), which was formerly the Skills Priority List, offers an annual point-in-time review of the status of Australian occupations. Specifically, the OSL reports on whether occupations (at the 4-digit and 6-digit ANZSCO level, and the 6-digit OSCA level) are experiencing shortages nationally and for each State and Territory in regional or metropolitan areas.

The OSL was last updated in 2025. The latest OSL differed from previous iterations due to the fact that in 2024 the ANZSCO classification framework for occupations was replaced with the OSCA framework. In terms of the 2025 OSL results, it was reported that 29 per cent of occupations (293 out of 1022 assessed) were in national shortage, which was 4 per cent lower than 2024 (33 per cent), and more than 7 per cent lower than 2023 (36 per cent). The OSL in 2025 also added 29 occupations newly in shortage compared to 2024, most of which were roles related to health, science, technicians and trades and machinery operators and drivers. As at February 2026, JSA had started the 2026 OSL survey but it had not yet confirmed a publication date for this year's list.

The OSL provided important context for stakeholder consultation preparation for the 2026 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report. This list indicates on a national level where specific occupation demands currently exist and enabled Public Skills Australia to proactively pursue conversations with Public Safety stakeholders on whether these demands exist within their contexts.

leadParagraphs: Public Skills Australia has built on the 2024 Workforce Plans and the 2025 Public Safety Workforce Insights Report in the development and delivery of this Report. These reports continue to be the strategic centrepiece guiding annual Business Plans for Public Skills Australia, alongside Ministerial, industry-sector and other priorities (e.g. Royal Commissions and Inquiries).
